title: How we onboarded 1,580 local businesses onto a Google co-pilot — what we learned
description:
The observation that kicked things off

In 2024 we spent three months talking to restaurant owners, hairdressers, mechanics and small artisans in Annecy, Lyon and Paris. One pattern came up everywhere: 90% of them knew their Google Business Profile was their best advertisement, and 90% had neither the time nor the skills to manage it seriously.

  • Customer reviews — nobody was replying ("I still have a negative review from 2021 with no response").
  • Websites — either non-existent or a WordPress patched together in 2016 that took 8 seconds to load.
  • Bookings — happening by SMS or phone, lost in the shuffle.
  • Social media? "I don't have the time."

On the tooling side, each problem had its own SaaS: Trustpilot or Partoo for reviews, Wix or Shopify for the site, Zenchef or Deliverect for bookings, Hootsuite for social. The bill: €150 to €400 per month, 6 logins, 6 invoices, and a shopkeeper who churns in 3 months.

Voxtya was born from that observation: put everything in one place, let the AI do 80% of the work, let the owner keep control in two clicks.

A year later, 1,580 local businesses trust us, 24,800 Google reviews have been collected through Voxtya, and our customers save an average of 9 hours per month while seeing +45% visits on their Google listing. Here's what we learned.

Lesson 1: the Google Business Profile is the #1 channel, but badly exploited

Before Voxtya, 68% of our customers had fewer than 15 Google reviews. After 6 months with us, that drops to 11%. The median goes from 12 to 47 reviews.

Why? Because asking for a review at the right time, from the right customer, through the right channel is a scriptwriter's job, not a restaurateur's. We built three mechanics that actually work in the real world:

  1. "Wheel of fortune" QR code stuck in the window or at the counter. The customer scans, spins the wheel (a small reward to win — a free coffee, dessert, discount), and to spin they're asked for a Google review. In restaurants with a terrace, scan rate exceeds 20%.
  2. SMS/email follow-up post-visit (for artisans and wellness especially): 24 hours after the service, a direct link to the Google listing.
  3. Room QR codes for hoteliers.

Aggregated result: ×3.9 review volume vs. pre-Voxtya, at constant advertising budget.

Lesson 2: replying to 100% of reviews within 48h changes everything

Google has said it repeatedly: businesses that reply to their reviews are favored in the local pack. We measured it on our customer base.

Across 170 businesses tracked over 6 months:

  • Those replying to <30% of reviews: flat local visibility.
  • Those replying to 100% of reviews within 48 hours (via our AI drafting the reply, validated or not by the owner): +28% impressions on the listing on average.

The detail that matters: the tone of the reply. Copy-paste replies ("thanks for your review") do nothing. Replies that pick up a word from the customer ("thanks for your feedback on our new truffle menu") convert three times better into action — click to directions, click to site, call.

That's exactly what the AI does, in 3 seconds, 24/7. The human keeps control of sensitive cases (complaints, 1 or 2 stars).

Lesson 3: a fast site derived from the Google listing beats a "designer" site

Half of our customers had no website. The other half had one they considered "not great". We tested a radical hypothesis: auto-generate the site from the Google listing (address, hours, photos, menu, services), with clean design, fast (<1s LCP), and perfect technical SEO.

Result:

  • Go-live time: 3 minutes, not 3 weeks.
  • PageSpeed mobile score: 91/100 average, vs. 38/100 for our customers' existing sites.
  • Organic traffic at 3 months: ×2.3 on queries like "bakery + city".

The trap we avoided: don't sell a "site builder". We sell a site already built the day they sign up, that the customer can modify if they want. 88% of our customers change nothing — and that's fine.

Lesson 4: online bookings must be free (for the end customer)

Zenchef, TheFork, Resy charge €2 to €7 per booking, or a monthly fee that bites. For a 40-seat restaurant with a €25 average ticket, that's 10% of margin lost to commission.

At Voxtya the booking module is included in the Suite, commission-free. The 280 restaurants we equip have moved all their bookings direct from their Voxtya site and Google listing. Over 6 months, that represents ~€94,000 of commissions not paid to TheFork in total.

For artisans, the "booking module" becomes a "quote request form" with automatic follow-ups. Same mechanics, same free.

Lesson 5: AI is useful when it hands back control fast, not when it fakes it

We almost got this wrong by trying to automate everything. Voxtya's first version published posts on Google Business Profile and Instagram without validation, from detected events (new menu, new photo). Owners hated it. "That's not my voice."

The right mechanic: the AI proposes (post draft, reply draft, new photo draft), the owner validates in 2 clicks from their phone. The draft has to be perfect 80% of the time for validation to feel like a reflex. Below that, the owner stops opening the app.

Today, 9 out of 10 owners validate without edits. But the ability to edit is central — it's what separates "copilot" from "autopilot". Local business owners don't want autopilot on their voice.

What doesn't work (let's be honest)

  • We don't have a solution for businesses without walk-in customers (wholesalers, B2B). The "window QR review collection" model doesn't apply.
  • Chains with more than 20 locations deserve a more enterprise-oriented tool; we point them elsewhere.
  • Onboarding is still too manual for some trades: an auto garage needs specific categories our generic configurator doesn't cover well yet.

If you're building your own tool

  • Start from the Google listing. It's the source of truth, not your internal DB.
  • Don't ask for the Google Business API login before the customer has seen value. Google makes onboarding painful; absorb it, don't push it to the customer.
  • AI should propose, not publish. 2-click validation, always.
  • Make free what your competitors charge for (bookings, websites). You'll earn it back on the monthly plan, not on commission.

If these takeaways are useful, the tool that came out of it is Voxtya — 30-day free trial, from €29 per month, no commitment.

title: Security Risks of AI-Generated Code: Research and a Review Checklist
description:
Originally published on shipfastdev.com.

AI-generated code usually works, but it is often not secure. In Veracode's 2026 tests, models produced code that compiled almost 100% of the time, yet failed security checks on nearly 44% of tasks, a pass rate that has not improved since 2025. The fix is not to ban AI tools; it is to treat their output like code from a contractor you have never worked with: review it, scan it, and test it before it reaches production.

Below is a summary of the research, the failure patterns that come up again and again, and a review checklist you can hand to your developer or agency.

What the research found

Veracode: about half of security-relevant tasks fail, and it is not improving

In its 2025 GenAI Code Security Report, Veracode gave 80 curated coding tasks to more than 100 large language models. When a secure and an insecure approach were both possible, models chose the insecure one 45% of the time. Java was the riskiest language, with a security failure rate above 70%; Python, C# and JavaScript failed between 38% and 45% of the time. Models failed to defend against cross-site scripting in 86% of cases and log injection in 88%. Larger models did not perform significantly better than smaller ones.

The 2026 edition found the average security pass rate "sits at 56 percent — virtually unchanged since last year's report." The best model on its summer 2026 leaderboard reached 68%, which still means failing nearly one security task in three. Python code passed 63% of the time, Java only 30%. Coding-specialised models (51%) did no better than general-purpose ones (52%), and model size made no clear difference, although reasoning models kept an edge (56% against 51%).

Academic studies: vulnerable suggestions and overconfident users

  • An early study of GitHub Copilot, "Asleep at the Keyboard?" (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022), generated 1,689 programs across 89 security-relevant scenarios and found approximately 40% of them vulnerable.
  • A user study published at ACM CCS 2023 found that participants with an AI assistant wrote significantly less secure code than those without, and were more likely to believe their code was secure.
  • A USENIX Security 2025 paper analysed 576,000 code samples from 16 models and found that at least 5.2% of packages suggested by commercial models and 21.7% by open-source models did not exist, with 205,474 unique invented package names. An attacker can publish a malicious package under a name that models tend to invent, and anyone who installs it without checking is compromised.

Team level: more changes, less stability

Google's 2025 DORA report found that AI adoption is linked to higher delivery throughput but still has a negative relationship with delivery stability. Its explanation applies directly to security: without strong automated testing and fast feedback loops, more change volume leads to more incidents.

Why AI-generated code fails security checks

Security usually depends on context the model does not have: which input comes from an untrusted user, who is allowed to see which record, which secrets exist in your environment. Cross-site scripting, which depends on knowing where a piece of data will be displayed, had one of the worst results in Veracode's 2025 tests (86% failure). The model writes code that does what you asked; whether it is safe depends on what you did not say.

The failure patterns to look for

  • Untrusted input reaching output or queries: cross-site scripting, SQL injection, log injection.
  • Missing authorisation checks: an endpoint that checks the user is logged in, but not that the record belongs to them.
  • Secrets in code: API keys pasted into source files or front-end bundles.
  • Invented or outdated dependencies: packages that do not exist, or old versions with known vulnerabilities.
  • Insecure defaults: permissive CORS, debug mode on, verbose error messages in production.
  • Weak cryptography or home-made auth instead of the framework's built-in tools.

A security review checklist for AI-generated code

You don't need to read code to use this list. Ask your developer to confirm each point for every feature that touches users, payments or data. Items 1 to 4 apply before any change is merged, 5 to 7 cover dependencies and secrets, and 8 to 12 cover testing and process.

  1. A human who understands the code has reviewed every AI-generated change, line by line.
  2. Every endpoint checks authorisation (who can access this record), not just authentication.
  3. All user input is validated on the server, and output is escaped by the framework (no raw HTML rendering of user content).
  4. Database access uses the framework's query builder or parameterised queries, never string-built SQL.
  5. Every new package was checked: it exists, is maintained, and is the one the developer meant to install.
  6. A dependency audit runs automatically (for example npm audit, composer audit or GitHub Dependabot).
  7. No secret is committed to the repository or shipped to the browser; secret scanning is enabled.
  8. Automated tests cover login, permissions and payment flows, and run on every change. End-to-end tests such as the Playwright setup we use catch broken access rules early.
  9. A static analysis (SAST) tool runs in CI on every pull request.
  10. Production runs with debug off, restrictive CORS and generic error pages.
  11. AI agents cannot touch production data or credentials directly.
  12. Someone owns security decisions, and you know who.

Questions to ask your developer or agency

  • Which AI tools do you use, and what is your review rule for their output?
  • What runs automatically on every pull request: tests, dependency audit, static analysis, secret scanning?
  • How are authorisation rules tested?
  • Who would notice if a new package did not exist yesterday?

These questions belong in any evaluation of a development partner. If your app was built mainly with an AI app builder, read where vibe-coded MVPs break as well: missing data-access rules are the most common problem there.

Frequently asked questions

Is AI-generated code secure?

Not by default. Veracode's 2026 tests found an average security pass rate of 56%, unchanged from 2025, even though almost all generated code compiled. It needs the same review and testing as any other code, and arguably more.

Which programming language is riskiest for AI-generated code?

In Veracode's tests, Java: a 30% security pass rate in 2026, against 63% for Python. Language matters less than review, though: every language failed a significant share of tasks.

Can an AI tool review its own code for security?

It can help spot issues, but the same models chose insecure options in a large share of Veracode's tasks. Use AI review as one layer, alongside static analysis, dependency audits, tests and a human reviewer.

Do I need a security audit for my MVP?

If it handles personal data, payments or logins, at least run through the checklist above before launch. A full external audit makes sense once you have real users or sensitive data at scale.

Sources

  1. LLMs Are Getting Smarter but Not Safer: Veracode 2026 GenAI Code Security Report, Veracode, 2026-07
  2. AI-Generated Code Poses Major Security Risks in Nearly Half of All Development Tasks, Veracode Research Reveals, Veracode, 2025-07
  3. Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions (IEEE S&P 2022), Pearce, Ahmad, Tan, Dolan-Gavitt, Karri (arXiv), 2021-12
  4. Do Users Write More Insecure Code with AI Assistants? (ACM CCS 2023), Perry, Srivastava, Kumar, Boneh (arXiv), 2023-12
  5. We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs (USENIX Security 2025), Spracklen et al. (arXiv), 2025-03
  6. Announcing the 2025 DORA Report, Google Cloud, 2025-09

title: A Backdoor Sat in the Firmware Partition of 1.3 Million Set-Top Boxes
description:
TL;DR

  • A botnet is a network of compromised devices that a remote operator controls, usually to rent out the devices or to run fraud at someone else's expense.
  • On 2 November 2026 Google Threat Intelligence Group disclosed that Google and its partners dismantled XCPE, a backdoor that enrolled more than 1.3 million Android set-top boxes, and attributed it with high confidence to Videostrong Technology, an Android OEM and ODM.
  • The backdoor sat in the firmware partition at android.uid.system privilege, reinstalled itself from the /oem/ partition when a user removed it, and handed module execution to a loader called com.abc.nexus.
  • Command and control runs in two stages: an HTTP POST that returns configuration, then a persistent MQTT connection to a broker that delivers app installs, shell commands, screen captures and network reconnaissance.
  • Affiliates bought a place on the device and loaded their own business models: residential proxy exit nodes such as Linkfog, AppSalt and NetNut, ad-fraud engines such as CBOXTV and HiddenView, and further backdoors.
  • The disruption cut off control domains, took down command servers used by more than a dozen affiliate malware families, and barred the vendor from certified Android devices; Google assesses it severs access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
  • A television box in a shop or an office that nobody inventories is an inventory problem, because firmware shipped in the factory cannot be patched remotely.
  • Detection leans on egress: look for long-lived MQTT sessions from devices that have no business holding one, and for downloads staged from operator-owned repositories.

Capture of the Google Cloud Threat Intelligence post “Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet”, taken 3 November 2026 from cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shutting-the-door-on-the-xcpe-botnet.

On 2 November 2026 Google Threat Intelligence Group published Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet, with the disclosure that Google and industry partners had dismantled a backdoor enrolled on more than 1.3 million set-top boxes. The attribution is the part that changes how the story should be read: the researchers assess with high confidence that the malware was developed, deployed and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology, an Android original equipment and original design manufacturer.

Videostrong built the backdoor into the firmware partition

The malicious software arrived preinstalled, across many device models and brands, built directly into firmware over multiple years. Google found dedicated infrastructure, evolving configurations and tools for managing affiliates, and assessed with high confidence that Videostrong intentionally developed, deployed and operated the backdoor and botnet for financial gain. Its response was to cut ties with Videostrong and ban the company from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Google's own account of how the code got past certification is worth reading twice. Certified Android devices pass a suite of compatibility and security tests, and the vendor used obfuscation to exploit a gap in those tests, loading malicious code after the device's first boot. Review processes changed as a result. For anyone who buys devices on the strength of a certification mark, this is the uncomfortable lesson: certification covers the tested state, and the vendor retains control over code loaded after first boot.

Netics editorial visual: the scale Google reported for the enrolled device population.

The stub runs at system privilege and hands execution to a loader

Three stages are documented, and the first one explains why removal fails. A stub package, shipped as x.cpe in some builds and com.oemservice in others, sits in the system partition and runs at android.uid.system privilege. On boot it checks the oem/ directory, installs the corresponding x.cpe package into /data/app/ and reinstalls itself after any user uninstall, which makes the device's own settings screen an unreliable place to look for the truth.

Stage two offloads the work. The backdoor acts mainly as the command-and-control communicator and passes module execution to com.abc.nexus, a file that carries native anti-analysis utilities to defeat sandbox detection and configures the monetisation modules. Since August 2026 that loader has been phased out in favour of tailored droppers that install a single module, delivered through the same command channel. Stage three is the modules themselves, arriving as native ELF daemons, as SDKs compiled into the loader's bytecode, or as secondary APKs fetched remotely. Google says a significant majority of the staging files—modules, shell scripts and legitimate applications—were hosted as GitHub releases on operator-owned GitHub pages.

Google Threat Intelligence Group figure, 2 November 2026: the XCPE ecosystem, from the infected set-top box and its backdoor through staging infrastructure to command servers and modules. Source: cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shutting-the-door-on-the-xcpe-botnet.

The command channel is an MQTT broker on the public internet

The command channel starts with HTTP and then moves to MQTT. The malware first sends an HTTP POST with an AES-encrypted JSON payload of hardware telemetry, serial number, MAC address, model and firmware version, to an operator host whose name is derived from the device's Android version and type. The response supplies MQTT broker details, including hostname, port, authentication token and the topic structure /device/{model}/{chipId}/{action}. From then on the device holds a persistent MQTT session, and MQTT is a publish-and-subscribe protocol built for low-bandwidth and unreliable networks, which describes consumer hardware well.

The same bootstrap returns geolocation and STUN parameters so the device can find its public address and traverse NAT, a file-upload URL for logs and diagnostic dumps, and switches for individual advertising modules. All samples analysed to that point used a single broker hostname, mqtt.szbboys[.]com. Command traffic that looks like ordinary telemetry and a broker reachable over the public internet describe a detection problem that lives in network logs, where most small organisations look last.

The affiliates paid for a place on the device and brought their own business models

The economic design is a rented shop window. Videostrong sold backdoor access to criminal affiliates, and the loaded modules turn the box into a residential proxy exit node, an ad-fraud engine, or a host for further backdoors. The named SDKs are specific: Linkfog, AppSalt and NetNut among the proxy networks, CBOXTV and HiddenView among the ad-fraud engines, Moyu and Spirit among the backdoors that load more modules. AppSalt is the residential proxy SDK owned by Honeygain, which is owned by Oxylabs, a detail that shows how ordinary the corporate chains behind these modules look.

Greed shows in the stacking. A single device can run several modules with the same function, and the researchers report as many as three residential proxy SDKs installed on one device. A compromised box becomes a metered egress point for someone else's traffic, with the household or office IP address carrying the reputation damage.

Netics editorial visual: the three-stage chain from firmware stub to monetisation module, and the step that ended it.

The partner list behind the disruption reads like a cross-section of the industry: Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI.

A device that cannot be patched is an inventory problem

This story turns firmware provenance into an inventory problem. A new image can fix a kernel or container flaw on every host that rebuilds. This backdoor was compiled into the firmware partition of devices already deployed in living rooms; the vendor is barred from certification and the hardware remains in the field.

Google's disruption made three moves worth noting for any operator. It took legal action against the domains and servers used to control the botnet and to install modules. It took legal action against command domains used by more than a dozen affiliate malware families, which the researchers assess severs access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, since those affiliates distribute through other channels too. And it changed how firmware integrity is verified on certified Android TV devices.

Devices keep reporting while the broker answers, so the distribution below shows where the installed base sits.

Google Threat Intelligence Group figure, 2 November 2026: the global distribution of devices reporting the x.cpe backdoor. Source: cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/shutting-the-door-on-the-xcpe-botnet.

The operator's version of that work starts with a list. Which Android boxes, signage players, conference-room dongles and kiosk displays are on the network, who bought them, which vendor built the firmware and whether that vendor still exists in a position to ship updates. Most small estates cannot answer the last question, and that gap is the exposure this campaign exploits.

What the disruption cut off, and what stays exposed

Google cut off command infrastructure and tightened firmware verification. Google took legal action to take down the domains, affiliate command servers are down, a manufacturer is out of the certified programme, and Google says it tightened firmware verification. A box already installed retains its backdoor. The researchers are explicit that the illicit market is resilient, with operators pivoting to new loaders or rival SDKs when a component is disrupted.

For a small organisation, the practical controls are unglamorous and cheap. Segment devices that need outbound internet from the rest of the network, deny egress to hosts nobody recognises, and watch for long-lived sessions to message brokers, which almost no television box needs. Prefer hardware whose firmware updates you can verify, and treat a bargain Android box from an unknown ODM as an untrusted endpoint with a screen attached. Prebuilt images carry their own provenance and inventory requirements. The earlier analysis of the Copy Fail container flaw argued from the software side; a full security audit and hardening is where an estate turns that reasoning into a list of devices it can defend.

“Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain.” The sentence closes the report, and it also describes the buying decision in front of any organisation refreshing its screens this quarter. The supply chain runs through the firmware partition, and the receipt is the only document most buyers keep.

Netics editorial visual: the report's closing framing, quoted from Google Threat Intelligence Group.

Originally published on the Netics blog.

title: In Zagreb, the company that owns the robotaxis chose the aggregator on day one
description:
On 26 March 2026 Uber, Verne and Pony.ai announced a three-way deal to bring robotaxis to Europe. Pony.ai supplies the autonomous driving, Croatian company Verne buys the cars and keeps them on the road, Uber brings the network. That same announcement already stated that rides would be bookable "via Uber as well as through Verne's app", and that Uber "intends to invest an undisclosed amount into Verne".

Two weeks later, on 8 April, Europe's first commercial robotaxi service started in Zagreb: Verne's app, about ninety square kilometres of the city including the airport, from seven in the morning to nine at night.

On 19 August the rides also appeared on Uber's app, with a licensed operator on board behind the wheel, Verne acting as fleet owner and service operator. On 10 September the first rides with nobody at the wheel began, on the twenty-two kilometres to the airport: test rides for invited passengers, while the commercial service kept the operator on board. On 7 October the investment was confirmed by Verne's chief executive, Marko Pejković: "I can confirm, yes, Uber has invested in Verne." The size of the stake was not disclosed.

The press covered the machine. For anyone coordinating a fleet, the thing to look at is different, and it is not an ambush: it is a choice. Europe's most advanced operator, the one that actually owns the driverless cars and has its own app, decided from day one to also go through the aggregator's app, and to let the aggregator into its capital.

If that is what the company with the robotaxis does, it is worth asking what a dispatch company will do: one with the shifts, the licences and thirty years of customers, but without a list to restart from.

The script has been written before, with today's cars

You do not need to wait for robotaxis to see how this ends. It has already happened twice, with human drivers.

August 2020: Uber buys Autocab, the British company that supplies booking and dispatch software to private hire operators, which is to say to its own competitors. On 29 March 2021 the UK competition authority closed its inquiry finding "no competition concerns", and the deal completed in April.

It is worth reading why it closed. The authority had considered exactly the data question, whether operators might be pushed into handing data to Uber, and set it aside by observing that there are "other credible suppliers" those operators "could switch" to if the service worsened or if data were demanded. In other words: in the authority's reasoning, the protection is not a promise, it is being able to leave.

The operators' main question at the time was the same one: what happens to our data. Autocab answered that it would handle them as always, without sharing. No abuse has emerged since, and that is not the point. The point is that the answer was a statement and not a clause, while the real guarantee had already been named by the regulator: the ability to walk away.

April 2025: Lyft buys FreeNow for 175 million euros. It was not buying cars. Ninety per cent of the gross bookings on that platform in 2024 came from taxis, which is to say from other people's vehicles and licences.

In both cases whoever was driving stayed at the wheel. What changed is who stands on the other side: in the first the supplier became the competitor, in the second the app changed owner.

Why the legal frame does not help here

In Italy the instinctive answer is that none of this applies yet, since the road code defines a vehicle as a machine "driven by a human" and a car that drives itself does not fit. Testing is nonetheless governed by the 2018 Smart Road decree.

But those rules defend the licence, not the relationship with the person getting into the car. No law obliges a passenger to call one number rather than another. Customers go where booking is easier, and they do not ask anyone's permission.

Original (Italian): A Zagabria anche l'operatore locale passa da Uber

Disclosure: I build UrbanGo, dispatch software for licensed taxi and private-hire operators. Everything above is sourced; this paragraph is the part where I sell something.

title: Scanning 525 Skills and 153 Claude Code & Codex Logs for Prompt-Injection & Repo-Open Traps
description:
The discussion on r/ClaudeAI (1xozfcv) about why 98% of the 16,060 open GitHub issues on anthropics/claude-code cannot simply be handed to autonomous triage agents hit on a real engineering problem: untrusted input poisoning.

Whenever you point Claude Code or Codex CLI at an external GitHub issue (gh issue view), a cloned PR branch, or a third-party SKILL.md file, four classes of traps can hijack the agent:

  1. Repo-open config hooks: .claude/settings.json (hooks, apiKeyHelper, statusLine), .mcp.json, or .vscode/tasks.json ("runOn": "folderOpen") inside a cloned repo that run commands on startup.
  2. Invisible Unicode steganography: Unicode Tag characters (U+E0000 to U+E007F), bidirectional overrides (U+202A to U+202E), and standalone zero-width spaces (U+200B).
  3. Spoofed <system-reminder> and </tool_result> delimiters inside untrusted issue bodies or web responses.
  4. Hidden HTML comment instructions & remote shell pipes (hidden HTML comment blocks with override instructions or curl ... | bash inside skill files).

Three false-positive traps and blind spots in my first scanner

When I ran my first scanner script across 525 local skill markdown files, 16 workspace repos, and 153 local Claude Code and Codex CLI transcripts, three things broke:

  1. Claude Code's 1,526 native type: "attachment" <system-reminder> rows: Scanning raw .jsonl lines for <system-reminder> to detect delimiter spoofing flagged 1,526 rows across 125 sessions because Claude Code writes its own internal system reminders as type: "attachment" and type: "api-request-*" records. Filtering out native attachment records (RTR012) isolated untrusted tool_result payloads (RTR008).
  2. Codex CLI's custom_tool_call_output nested object payloads (142 zero-width characters across 5 sessions): Unlike function_call_output (where payload.output is a string), Codex CLI's custom_tool_call_output stores payload.output as a nested JSON object. My initial String(payload.output) call turned the tool output into "[object Object]" and missed 138 of the 142 standalone U+200B and U+200E characters ingested across 15 tool outputs (RTR011).
  3. Composite Emoji U+200D ZWJ vs standalone U+200B (RTR014): A raw zero-width regex flagged composite emojis (1 in notebook-guidance/SKILL.md) until I separated Emoji Zero-Width Joiner sequences (<Emoji> U+200D <Emoji>) from standalone U+200B spaces (2 in signs-of-ai-writing.md, RTR007) and 1 live curl -fsSL https://composio.dev/install | bash remote shell pipe in composio-cli/SKILL.md (RTR005).

Running repotrap

I published the zero-dependency scanner as repotrap (npx repotrap):

npx repotrap

You can also pre-scan a live GitHub issue or PR via the gh-issue option (npx repotrap with gh-issue owner/repo#123) before letting an agent read it, or run emit-hook mode to generate a deterministic PostToolUse sanitizer hook for ~/.claude/settings.json.

Limitations

  • repotrap deterministically catches invisible Unicode (U+E0000 tags, Bidi overrides, standalone U+200B), spoofed XML/system delimiters, hidden HTML comment instructions, curl | sh skill pipes, and .claude/.mcp.json/.vscode repo-open hooks. It cannot prove whether plain natural-language prose without structural markers or override phrases will sway a model.

GitHub: https://github.com/princejain756/repotrap
npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/repotrap

title: I Verified Sakura AI Engine's Free Tier: 3 Models, 3 Tasks, Honest Results
description:
1. Introduction

When I evaluate an LLM API for work, two worries come first.

  • Will I get billed without noticing while "just trying" the free tier?
  • Will my input text be stored or used for training?

Sakura AI Engine, a Japanese cloud service by Sakura Internet, answers both on its official pages. It states a zero data retention (ZDR) policy — inputs are neither stored nor used for training — and offers a free plan with 3,000 chat requests per month.

On November 6, 2026, I ran three models from the free plan through the same three tasks in the web Playground, then checked every answer by eye and by independent calculation. Here is what I found.

2. What the free plan actually includes

From the official product page:

  • Chat Completions: free up to 3,000 requests per month. Past that, requests are rate-limited — there is no automatic billing
  • ZDR: input data is not stored and not used for training. Processing runs in data centers in Japan
  • The Chat Completions catalog lists 10 models. One of them (a medical model) is outside the free tier, so 9 models are free to try
  • RAG is outside the free tier and billed by usage (3 JPY per 100 chunks)

A common misconception

A "free plan" does not mean everything is free. RAG and the medical model are excluded. Check the scope before you build on it.

3. How I verified

I used the Playground with a fresh conversation for each trial, one submission per model per task, and no retries.

Models: gpt-oss-120b / llm-jp-3.1-8x13b-instruct4 / preview/Kimi-K2.6
Task 1 (explanation): explain RAG for non-experts in 450 characters or fewer
Task 2 (code): a Python moving_average(values, window) function plus unittest cases.
               Expected values for [2,4,6,8,10] with window=4 and 5 had to be
               derived independently from the sublists
Task 3 (summary): summarize a municipal energy-saving text in exactly 3 bullets,
               without adding numbers that are not in the source
Settings: Playground defaults (temperature and token limits not verified)

I did not execute any generated code. I checked the test expectations with my own arithmetic, independently of the models. I did not measure time to first token or token counts.

A common misconception

A model's own "reasoning" is not verification. In this run, one model confidently explained wrong expected values as if they were correct. Always cross-check with an independent method.

4. Results

4.1 Explanation (RAG)

All three models separated the roles of retrieval and generation, and noted that having sources does not guarantee correctness.

Kimi-K2.6 was concise and split its caveats into two kinds: the source documents themselves can be wrong, and the AI can misinterpret or miscombine them. gpt-oss-120b also covered how to check sources, although one claim — that real-time intake makes answers comprehensive — was stronger than the conditions justify.

llm-jp-3.1-8x13b-instruct4 ignored the 450-character limit and answered in long paragraphs. The content was not far off, but the requested form and length were not followed.

4.2 Code generation

The correct expected values, from my own calculation:

[2,4,6,8,10], window=4 -> [5, 7]   ((2+4+6+8)/4=5, (4+6+8+10)/4=7)
[2,4,6,8,10], window=5 -> [6]

gpt-oss-120b and Kimi-K2.6 produced functions, tests, and expected values that all matched the independent calculation. Kimi-K2.6 provided 10 tests, including one that the input list is not modified.

llm-jp-3.1-8x13b-instruct4 wrote a function that visually matched the spec, but several expected values in its tests were wrong:

  • window=4 expected 5, 6, 7, 8, 9
  • window=5 expected [4, 6, 8, 10], and [6, 8, 10] on another line (correct: [6])
  • [2,4,6] with window=4 expected 4, 6
  • Its explanation then justified the wrong values, and the input-immutability test was missing

Since I did not execute the code, this only establishes whether the expected values were right — not whether the code runs.

4.3 Summarization

I scored the summaries against nine elements of the source text: 20 facilities in 2024, 1.2M kWh total with the 55/30/15 split, LED and air-conditioning measures, a 12% year-over-year decrease, the hot-day room-temperature problem, continued measurement, the 24M JPY cost, payback period undetermined due to electricity price fluctuation, and the caution against generalizing single-year numbers.

Kimi-K2.6 returned exactly three bullets, kept all nine elements, and added no numbers of its own.

gpt-oss-120b kept all nine elements but added figures that are not in the source: 660k / 360k / 180k kWh. The arithmetic behind them is correct, but the instruction was to add nothing.

llm-jp-3.1-8x13b-instruct4 answered in a single paragraph instead of three bullets and dropped a few points, including the hot-day condition.

A common misconception

Each model ran each task exactly once. These results are not a ranking. Read them as concrete examples of each model's habits.

5. What the earlier round showed

In past records from an earlier round on the same day (9 models × 3 tasks, 27 trials), similar habits appeared:

  • One model reversed "do not generalize" into "generalize" in its summary
  • One model swapped the facility ratios
  • One small model's generated tests had every expected value wrong (the only execution evidence in those records is a single input run of an older Qwen function)

Combining both rounds, the weak point is not fluency. It is faithfulness to numbers and meaning. Expected values and summaries only become usable after an independent check.

6. Limitations

  • I have not verified the APIs yet. OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoint checks, and Claude Code integration, are still to come
  • I did not execute the generated code, so I cannot claim it works or that any test passes
  • I did not measure TTFT or token counts, and I am not comparing speed
  • After the trials, the usage display showed 37 requests and 0 JPY. That is 7 more than the 9 submissions I recorded, so treat the 0 JPY as a display observation, not a confirmed final bill
  • One tested model is a preview offering and may be discontinued or changed without notice

7. Summary

Within the free plan, you can try 9 models with no billing risk, and the ZDR policy is stated in writing. As an evaluation entry point, the conditions are solid.

Quality, however, varies by task and by model. In this run, skipping the cross-check on expected values and summary details would have carried errors straight into real work.

Next, I will verify the API endpoints and the Claude Code integration, and update this post with the results.

8. References

  • Sakura AI Engine official site (free plan terms, model list, and the "input data is not used for training or stored" policy): https://ai.sakura.ad.jp/sakura-ai/ai-engine/
  • Zennfes Autumn 2026, Sakura division (the contest this post is entered in): https://zenn.dev/contests/zennfes-autumn-2026-sakura
  • Sakura Internet official announcement (2026-11-02): https://www.sakura.ad.jp/corporate/information/announcements/2026/11/02/1968226190/

title: Silent failures in agentic systems: when retry and fallback fake an OK
description:
No alert isn't no problem. Silent retry and fallback return "OK" while quality tanks. Datadog: 1/3 of LLM errors are hidden rate-limits.

Father's Day taught me one brutal truth: when a house goes suspiciously quiet, it doesn't mean there's peace. It means a kid just did something. In agentic systems engineering it works exactly the same way. Quiet is not proof of health. Sometimes it's proof that something already went wrong, and nobody shouted.

Systems that "heal themselves"

Most of you build systems with a survival instinct baked in. Request failed? Retry. Model threw an error? Fall back to a cheaper model. All silent, no bells, no alerts. It sounds like good agentic engineering, and sometimes it is. The trouble starts when that mechanism becomes the system's only reaction and leaves no trace behind.

From the outside it looks like success, because the system returns "OK". Status 200, there's a response, the dashboard is green. Underneath, quality is nosediving. The retry only worked on the third try, on a different, weaker model. The fallback quietly swapped the context. The user got an answer a whole class worse, and nobody found out, because no light ever came on.

Why do we build it this quiet in the first place? Because every one of us has been jolted awake at 3 a.m. by an alert that turned out to be nothing. Alert fatigue is real, so we instinctively mute anything that "sorts itself out". But there's a chasm between "don't page me for a single retry" and "don't log the retry at all". The first is hygiene. The second is blindness. And blindness is exactly where silent failures come from, the kind nobody can explain afterwards.

A third of errors are rate-limits swept under the rug

The Datadog State of AI Engineering 2026 report leaves no room for illusions: 1/3 of all errors in LLM spans are rate-limits that a "silent retry" sweeps under the rug. One in three. That's not statistical noise, it's a systematic signal that your infrastructure keeps hitting limits and you can't see it, because the retry patches the hole before anyone notices it's there.

No alert isn't the same as no problem. They're two completely different things, and they're very easy to confuse. A rate limit that's quietly retried today will stop fitting inside the window tomorrow, under heavier traffic. And then "silent" gets very loud. At the worst possible moment, exactly when you need stability the most.

And here's the crux: a rate limit isn't a random fault, it's a capacity question. If a third of your errors are throughput limits you can't see, you don't have a model problem. You have a planning problem. Another retry won't fix that. A deliberate decision will: more quota, a queue, or backpressure that someone actually sees on a chart.

"Silence in the logs is the loudest signal that your agent stopped working and started pretending."

Retry and fallback aren't automation. They're debt.

If your system retries or drops to a fallback and leaves no counter, no log, no trace at all in your monitoring, you don't have automation. You have hidden tech debt. The kind that stays quiet until it grows, then blows up in your face. You end up building systems that lie about being healthy because they're scared to shout.

The difference between mature AI observability and theatre is dead simple: every retry and every fallback has to be countable. The point isn't to get rid of them. They're a normal part of a resilient system. The point is that each one leaves a trace you can count, chart, and wake an alert with. It sounds like extra work, but it's a few lines in a layer you already have. The same logic works on a model's judgments: two independent questions about the same thing, and then a contradiction between the answers, is the cheapest detector there is for a result that looks right and isn't.

Silence costs you in another way too, not just in uptime. If someone plants an instruction in content the agent fetches by itself, the only trace left behind is a tool call nobody counts. What that attack looks like from the inside, and which tools an agent should lose first, is in the post on instructions hidden in the content an agent fetches on its own.

A TRACE INSTEAD OF SILENCE

  • A retry counter. How many times, on which step, with which error code. Not one lumped-together "errors" number.
  • A fallback event. From which model, to which, and why. Otherwise you don't know whose quality you just dropped.
  • Rate limits as their own metric. Not "an error that fixed itself", but something you watch grow.
  • Alert on the trend. Not on a single retry, but on the week-over-week rise. The trend is what gives a silent failure away.

On the business side the same requirement goes by another name, audit trail, and it's one of the four pillars of bounded autonomy. Same thing, two vocabularies: the engineer counts retries, the board asks who made the decision and on what basis.

A silent failure wears many faces. Sometimes it's a retry, sometimes a fallback, and sometimes a model that grades its own work and hands itself an A. I wrote about that second trap, the model that confuses confidence with correctness, in a separate post on model self-evaluation. The mechanism is exactly the same: the system returns "OK" because nobody forced it to admit it was wrong.

Count your silent failures

Go into your monitoring today and count how many times in the last week something quietly retried or dropped to a fallback. A real number, not "a few, probably". If you can't give that number, you just found your silent failure. The first step isn't the fix. The first step is seeing it at all.

If that count comes back and you cannot say what your agent quietly does in production, that is the first question of an agent risk audit: what it can reach, what it can execute without a person, and what happens when that fails.

SOURCES

  • Datadog: State of AI Engineering 2026 (~1/3 of errors in LLM spans are rate-limits)

Originally published at szymonpaluch.com.

title: Agences IA et cabinets de recrutement dans dix villes : Claude lit les annuaires, GPT lit les sites
description:
Quand on demande à un assistant IA de recommander un prestataire dans une ville, d'où vient sa liste ? Nous avons posé la même question à Claude et à GPT, ville par ville, pour deux métiers : les agences IA et les cabinets de recrutement. Deux relevés, faits à un jour d'intervalle avec le même protocole, qui donnent le même résultat. Nous les présentons ensemble.

Le protocole

La question. Identique partout, avec le nom de la ville : « Je cherche une agence IA pour une PME à Lyon. Quelles entreprises me recommandes-tu, et pourquoi ? » La version recrutement remplace « une agence IA » par « un cabinet de recrutement ».

Les villes. Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Lille, Nantes, Strasbourg, Rennes et Nice.

Les questions en plus. Pour les agences IA, deux questions à l'échelle de la France : l'une sur les agences IA, l'autre sur les agences GEO, qui travaillent la place d'une entreprise dans les réponses des IA. Soit 12 questions pour les agences IA et 10 pour le recrutement.

Les modèles. Claude interrogé par Claude Code, GPT par Codex, tous deux avec recherche web. Chaque question est posée une fois à chaque IA : dans la nuit du 23 au 24 octobre 2026 pour les agences IA, les 24 et 25 octobre pour le recrutement.

Le rapprochement des noms. Les noms sont comparés après normalisation : minuscules, accents, ponctuation, formes juridiques. Pour le recrutement, un cabinet cité dans plusieurs réponses est compté une fois quand son site est le même.

Le comptage des sources. Une source par réponse et par site, parmi celles que l'IA cite.

Résultat 1 : deux IA, deux listes

Agences IA Cabinets de recrutement
Réponses 24 20
Noms différents cités 65 73
Villes sans aucun nom en commun 6 sur 10 7 sur 10
Villes avec un nom en commun 4 1 (Lyon)
Villes avec deux noms en commun 0 2 (Nantes et Nice)

Pour les agences IA, les IA citent environ trois noms par réponse. Sur les deux questions à l'échelle de la France, Claude et GPT n'ont aucun nom en commun non plus. Pour le recrutement, Claude cite près de cinq cabinets par réponse, GPT un peu plus de trois.

Les listes sont aussi très dispersées d'une ville à l'autre :

  • agences IA : une agence revient dans cinq villes, une autre dans trois, les autres ne sont citées que dans une seule ville ;
  • recrutement : un cabinet revient dans cinq villes, trois autres dans deux villes, les 69 autres dans une seule ville.

Résultat 2 : Claude lit des annuaires, GPT lit les sites des entreprises

C'est le résultat le plus net, et il se répète d'un métier à l'autre.

Sources citées par Claude

Type de source Agences IA Recrutement
Classements, listes ou annuaires 28 26
Sites des entreprises 14 5
Fiches Indeed ou pages d'avis non distinguées 6
Autres sources 12 4

Sources citées par GPT

Type de source Agences IA Recrutement
Sites des entreprises 37 33
Autres sources 1 0

Côté Claude, un annuaire domine à chaque fois. Pour les agences IA, il s'appuie sur La Fabrique du Net dans 10 de ses 12 réponses, sur ses pages d'agences d'intelligence artificielle par région ; il cite aussi Sortlist dans 4 réponses, et des comparateurs d'outils IA. Pour le recrutement, il s'appuie sur l'annuaire des cabinets de recrutement de Blog RH dans ses 10 réponses, et cite dans 8 réponses une liste des « meilleurs cabinets de recrutement » de la ville publiée par un autre site.

Côté GPT, les sources sont presque toutes les sites des entreprises recommandées : 37 sur 38 pour les agences IA, 33 sur 33 pour le recrutement. Il lit leurs pages de services, leurs références, leurs pages d'agence par ville ou leurs pages sur le recrutement en PME.

Ce que nous en retenons

Les deux assistants ne cherchent pas au même endroit. Chez Claude, un ou deux annuaires reviennent dans presque toutes les réponses. Chez GPT, la page d'une entreprise qui dit clairement son métier, sa ville et ses clients fait le travail.

Pour une entreprise qui veut être citée, cela fait deux chantiers séparés : une fiche complète sur les annuaires que lit Claude, avec son métier et sa ville, et une page de son propre site qui répond à la question telle qu'un client la pose. Pour qui mesure cette visibilité, la conséquence est la même que dans notre relevé sur 35 PME : interroger chaque assistant séparément et relever les sources, qui disent quoi travailler.

Limites

  • Une seule exécution par question et par IA. Les réponses d'un assistant changent d'un jour à l'autre.
  • Outils en ligne de commande. Claude passe par Claude Code et GPT par Codex. Les réponses peuvent différer de celles de claude.ai ou de ChatGPT.
  • Rapprochement des noms imparfait. Deux variantes d'un même nom peuvent échapper à la normalisation, ce qui gonflerait le nombre de noms différents et réduirait les noms en commun.
  • Sources visibles seulement. Nous comptons les sources que les IA citent dans leur réponse ; nous ne savons pas tout ce qu'elles ont lu.
  • Deux métiers, dix villes. Le partage des sources se répète sur les deux métiers et sur notre relevé de 35 PME, ce qui ne prouve pas qu'il vaut pour tous les métiers.
  • Les noms des agences et des cabinets recommandés ne sont pas publiés.

Les deux études complètes, avec la façon de les citer, sont publiées sur notre site : Quelles agences IA Claude et GPT recommandent aux PME, dans dix villes et Quels cabinets de recrutement Claude et GPT recommandent aux PME, dans dix villes. Le relevé sur 35 PME de services : Ce que Claude et GPT recommandent quand on cherche le métier de 35 PME.

Alta36 installe pour les PME françaises de 10 à 50 personnes une mémoire d'entreprise et des agents IA pour la direction, la prospection, le contenu et le CRM.

title: Building VARYN: Why Permission Boundaries Matter More Than Another AI API Call
description:
I started building VARYN because I wanted to explore a practical question: how much control should a user have over an AI workspace before it sends data to external models or performs actions?

Connecting an application to an LLM API is relatively straightforward. Building a workspace that makes permissions, costs, and failure conditions visible is a different engineering problem.

VARYN is my open-source experiment in addressing that problem.
The first challenge was separating a user's intent from permission to execute it.

A model request should not automatically imply permission to transmit data or spend API credits.

In VARYN's current Model Control Center, the owner selects a provider and model, reviews estimated pricing, and explicitly approves the outgoing request.

The supported API routes include OpenRouter, DeepSeek, and an optional local 9Router gateway.

The application also includes a fake-model mode for testing the interaction without making an external API call.

An important limitation: Estimated pricing is not a provider-enforced spending cap. The application cannot guarantee the final bill.
I also wanted tasks to persist beyond a single UI session.

The current implementation uses SQLite for local task storage, including task creation, status changes, pagination, and due-date tracking.

The task store doesn't impose an artificial global limit on the number of saved tasks, although disk capacity and database constraints still apply.

What it doesn't do yet is equally important: marking a task as due doesn't automatically execute an external workflow.

This distinction helps keep a task tracker from being presented as a fully autonomous scheduling system.
Another area I explored was organizing potential application integrations.

VARYN currently has a directory of connector, plugin, and skill candidates.

However, displaying a service in a directory doesn't mean the user has authenticated it.

A real connector needs its own supported authentication mechanism, permission scopes, error handling, and revocation process.

The current catalog makes this limitation explicit rather than implying that existing ChatGPT connections can be inherited by an unrelated application.
The desktop is built with Python and Tkinter.

I created a portable Windows x64 build through GitHub Actions, with the Python runtime bundled so the application doesn't require a separate Python installation.

The pipeline includes Windows and Ubuntu checks, along with packaging and hosted Windows GUI verification.

That evidence is useful, but it isn't the same as validating every interaction on a real end-user machine.

The current binary remains unsigned and experimental.
VARYN is not a finished universal AI agent.

The larger engineering challenges include durable multi-step execution, authenticated third-party connectors, safe action recovery, stronger local data protection, and a more cohesive model-memory-tool workflow.

Native two-way synchronization with the consumer ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini apps is also not a capability I can claim today.

These are meaningful engineering boundaries, not just missing checkboxes on a feature list.
The first Windows alpha is available publicly, along with its source code and implementation notes.

GitHub: https://github.com/naraya07pedro-spec/VARYN

I'd particularly value feedback from engineers working on agent runtimes, API integrations, permission systems, and local-first applications.

If you were reviewing this project, which architectural risk would you address first?

title: Pourquoi git checkout ne peut-il pas annuler ce qu'un agent de code IA a modifié ?
description:
Quand un agent IA modifie des fichiers de votre projet et casse quelque chose, le réflexe est git checkout -- . ou git stash. Les deux répondent à une autre question que la vôtre. Git peut vous ramener au dernier commit. Ce que vous voulez, c'est le dossier tel qu'il était juste avant le tour de l'agent, avec votre propre travail non commité et les fichiers que git ignore, et sans les fichiers que l'agent a créés.

L'application de bureau osFoundry règle ça avec un petit stockage adressé par contenu écrit en Rust, checkpoint_store.rs. Avant qu'une écriture de l'agent n'atteigne un fichier, les octets actuels du fichier sont sauvegardés sous <project>/.osfoundry/checkpoints/blobs/<sha256>, et /rewind les réécrit. Voici la même conception en environ 90 lignes de Python avec uniquement la bibliothèque standard, confrontée à quatre recettes git sur un tour réaliste, et chronométrée sur une copie d'une vraie arborescence de sources TypeScript de 4,686 fichiers.

Un tour, cinq façons de l'annuler

Le projet de test est un tout petit site dans un dépôt git : index.html, styles.css (212 lignes), app.js, et un .env exclu par .gitignore. Après le dernier commit, l'utilisateur a changé le titre de la page dans index.html et commencé un notes.md non suivi. C'est l'état auquel il faut revenir.

Vient ensuite le tour de l'agent : il réécrit styles.css pour le ramener à 41 lignes, modifie index.html pour charger un nouveau theme.css, réécrit app.js, fait pointer API_URL dans .env vers localhost, et crée theme.css. Chaque méthode d'annulation a tourné sur une copie fraîche, et un script a comparé chaque fichier octet par octet avec l'état d'avant le tour.

checkpoint restore                 matches the state before the turn: True   differs: []
git checkout -- .                  matches the state before the turn: False  differs: ['.env', 'index.html', 'theme.css']
git stash -u                       matches the state before the turn: False  differs: ['.env', 'index.html', 'notes.md']
git checkout + git clean -fd       matches the state before the turn: False  differs: ['.env', 'index.html', 'notes.md']
git stash create before the turn   matches the state before the turn: False  differs: ['.env', 'theme.css']
Méthode Ce qui ne va pas
git checkout -- . La modification du titre par l'utilisateur est perdue avec celles de l'agent, theme.css reste, .env garde la valeur de l'agent
git stash -u Les changements de l'agent, la modification du titre par l'utilisateur et notes.md partent tous ensemble dans un même stash, et .env garde la valeur de l'agent
git checkout + git clean -fd theme.css est supprimé, mais notes.md aussi, la modification du titre a disparu, et .env garde la valeur de l'agent
git stash create avant le tour Tout ce qui est suivi revient, mais theme.css reste et .env n'est jamais dans l'instantané
restauration du checkpoint Correspond à l'état d'avant le tour

Les résultats de git découlent de ce qu'est git. Il restaure le dernier commit, ou un instantané des fichiers suivis et indexés, et les deux mélangent votre travail avec celui de l'agent dès que ni l'un ni l'autre n'est commité. Les fichiers ignorés lui sont invisibles sauf si vous ajoutez -a, et un checkout ne supprime jamais un fichier qui n'existait pas dans l'instantané. La dernière ligne correspond à la configuration git la plus équitable, un instantané pris avant chaque tour, et elle rate quand même deux des cinq fichiers. Elle a aussi un effet de bord : git add -A indexe tout votre travail dans le vrai index à chaque tour.

Le stockage

Un checkpoint est une liste par tour : pour chaque fichier écrit par l'agent, soit le hash de son ancien contenu, soit une note indiquant qu'il n'existait pas. Les octets vont dans blobs/ une seule fois par contenu distinct.

import hashlib, json, os, time
from pathlib import Path

MAX_BLOB = 8 * 1024 * 1024

class Checkpoints:
    def __init__(self, root):
        self.root = Path(root).resolve()
        self.dir = self.root / ".osfoundry" / "checkpoints"
        self.blobs = self.dir / "blobs"
        self.index_file = self.dir / "index.json"
        try:
            self.index = json.loads(self.index_file.read_text())
        except (OSError, ValueError):
            self.index = []

    def _save(self):
        self.dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        tmp = self.dir / "index.json.tmp"
        tmp.write_text(json.dumps(self.index))
        os.replace(tmp, self.index_file)  # a half-written index loses everything

    def capture(self, turn, label, path):
        path = str(Path(path).resolve()) if Path(path).exists() else str(Path(path).absolute())
        if not self._contained(path):
            raise ValueError("outside the workspace: " + path)
        cp = next((c for c in self.index if c["turn"] == turn), None)
        if cp and any(f["path"] == path for f in cp["files"]):
            return                      # first write in a turn wins
        try:
            size = os.path.getsize(path)
        except FileNotFoundError:
            pre = {"kind": "absent"}
        else:
            if size > MAX_BLOB:
                pre = {"kind": "skipped", "reason": f"{size >> 20} MB over the limit"}
            else:
                data = Path(path).read_bytes()
                sha = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
                blob = self.blobs / sha
                if not blob.exists():   # identical bytes are stored once
                    self.blobs.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                    blob.write_bytes(data)
                pre = {"kind": "content", "sha256": sha, "bytes": size}
        entry = {"path": path, "pre": pre}
        if cp:
            cp["files"].append(entry)
        else:
            self.index.append({"turn": turn, "label": label[:120],
                               "at": time.time_ns(), "files": [entry]})
        self._save()

    def write(self, turn, label, path, data):
        """What an agent's write tool would call."""
        self.capture(turn, label, path)
        Path(path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        Path(path).write_bytes(data)

Trois détails décident si une restauration est correcte, et chacun est aussi une règle dans le module Rust.

La première capture d'un chemin dans un tour l'emporte. Un agent écrit souvent le même fichier plusieurs fois dans un tour. Revenir en arrière, c'est retrouver le fichier tel qu'il était au début du tour, pas un état intermédiaire entre deux écritures de l'agent lui-même ; les captures suivantes du même chemin dans le même tour sont donc ignorées.

Un fichier absent est enregistré comme absent. C'est cette seule ligne qui permet à une restauration de supprimer theme.css. Git n'a pas d'équivalent pour « ce fichier ne doit pas exister », à part un git clean qui supprime aussi des fichiers que vous vouliez garder.

Les fichiers de plus de 8 MB sont enregistrés comme skipped avec une raison, au lieu d'être laissés de côté. Une restauration signale alors qu'elle n'a pas pu les remettre, au lieu de se terminer en silence avec un mélange d'anciens et de nouveaux fichiers.

Restaurer, du plus ancien au plus récent 

    def restore(self, turn):
        target = next(c["at"] for c in self.index if c["turn"] == turn)
        affected = sorted((c for c in self.index if c["at"] >= target),
                          key=lambda c: c["at"])          # oldest first
        done, report = set(), {"restored": [], "deleted": [], "failed": []}
        for cp in affected:
            for f in cp["files"]:
                path, pre = f["path"], f["pre"]
                if path in done:
                    continue
                done.add(path)
                if not self._contained(path):            # re-check, the index is just a file
                    report["failed"].append((path, "outside the workspace"))
                elif pre["kind"] == "skipped":
                    report["failed"].append((path, pre["reason"]))
                elif pre["kind"] == "absent":
                    Path(path).unlink(missing_ok=True)
                    report["deleted"].append(path)
                else:
                    Path(path).parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
                    Path(path).write_bytes((self.blobs / pre["sha256"]).read_bytes())
                    report["restored"].append(path)
        self.index = [c for c in self.index if c["at"] < target]
        self._save()
        return report

    def _contained(self, path):
        p = Path(path)
        if ".." in p.parts:
            return False
        p = p if p.is_absolute() else self.root / p
        while not p.exists():          # deepest existing ancestor, symlinks resolved
            p = p.parent
        return p.resolve().is_relative_to(self.root)

Revenir au tour 1 alors que les tours 2 et 3 ont suivi doit annuler les trois. Restaurer seulement le tour 1 laisserait des fichiers du tour 2 à côté de fichiers d'avant le tour 1, une combinaison qui n'a jamais existé. L'ordre compte aussi. Pour un fichier touché dans plusieurs tours, les bons octets sont la pré-image la plus ancienne, celle capturée au début du tour 1. Parcourir du plus récent au plus ancien tombe sur la pré-image du tour 2, qui est l'état produit par le tour 1. Le code Rust contient un commentaire précisément là-dessus : il a d'abord été écrit du plus récent au plus ancien, et le test rewinding_a_turn_also_undoes_later_turns l'a détecté.

La vérification du chemin est refaite au moment de la restauration parce que index.json est un simple fichier dans le dossier qu'il décrit. Si on lui faisait confiance, n'importe qui ou n'importe quoi capable de le modifier pourrait faire écrire une restauration n'importe où sur le disque. Les tours annulés sont ensuite retirés de l'index, pour qu'un second retour au même point ne puisse pas « réussir » sur des fichiers déjà revenus.

Ce que ça coûte sur un vrai dossier

L'arborescence est une copie du dossier src d'une vraie application React et TypeScript : 4,686 fichiers, 121.4 MB, aucun fichier au-dessus de 8 MB. À chaque tour, des fichiers ont été choisis au hasard, capturés, puis on leur a ajouté une ligne ; ensuite une restauration a tourné et chaque fichier a été comparé à l'original. Toutes les restaurations correspondaient. Apple M1, 8 GB, macOS 15, SSD APFS, Python 3.9.6, git 2.39.5.

Tour Capture + écriture Taille du stockage Restauration
4 fichiers + 1 créé 3.5 ms moins de 0.1 MB 1.2 ms
50 fichiers + 1 créé 62.4 ms 0.9 MB 8.2 ms
500 fichiers + 1 créé 1,035 ms 11.7 MB 227 ms
les 4,686 fichiers 30.5 s 122.7 MB 1.3 s

À titre de comparaison, l'instantané git par tour du scénario ci-dessus (git add -A puis git stash create) a pris 61 à 68 ms sur cette arborescence sans aucun changement, et 50 à 67 ms avec quatre fichiers modifiés. Il doit examiner les 4,686 fichiers à chaque fois. Juste après l'exécution qui avait réécrit tous les fichiers, la suivante a pris 1,241 ms, parce que git recalcule le hash de chaque fichier dont l'horodatage a changé. Un checkpoint ne regarde jamais que les fichiers en cours d'écriture, donc un tour normal coûte quelques millisecondes, quelle que soit la taille du projet.

La dernière ligne révèle un problème dans le code tel qu'il est écrit. La capture moyenne a pris 1.29 ms pour les 100 premiers fichiers du tour et 9.54 ms pour les 100 derniers. Chaque capture réécrit tout le fichier index.json, qui a atteint 1.3 MB, donc le coût de chaque écriture augmente avec le nombre d'écritures précédentes. Remplacer _save par l'ajout d'une ligne JSON par capture a réglé le problème sur les mêmes 4,686 fichiers : 2.5 s au total, 0.41 ms par capture au début et 0.61 ms à la fin. Pour un agent qui modifie une poignée de fichiers par tour, la version simple suffit. Pour un formateur ou un renommage sur toute la base de code passé par un agent, utilisez le journal en ajout seul.

Ce que l'adressage par contenu fait gagner, et ce qu'il ne fait pas gagner

Nommer les blobs par leur SHA-256 déduplique les octets identiques et rien d'autre. Trois mesures montrent ce que ça donne.

Sur toute l'arborescence, 4,686 fichiers avaient 4,677 contenus distincts, donc un tour sur l'arborescence complète a stocké 4,677 blobs. Les fichiers en double sont rares dans une vraie arborescence de sources.

Un fichier de 2 MB réécrit sur dix tours, l'agent ajoutant une ligne à chaque fois : dix pré-images, toutes différentes, 10 blobs et 20.0 MB. Même fichier, mais l'agent écrit les mêmes octets à chaque tour, comme le fait une nouvelle tentative qui produit une sortie identique : 2 blobs et 4.0 MB, l'original et la version dont partait chaque tour suivant. Dans les deux cas, revenir au premier tour a rendu l'original octet par octet.

Les blobs sont stockés bruts. Les 121.4 MB de blobs du tour sur l'arborescence complète feraient 33.7 MB avec zlib au niveau 6, et le propre stockage d'objets de git pour la même arborescence après un commit faisait 41.0 MB. La compression est un ajout raisonnable si le stockage est conservé longtemps, puisque le code source se compresse à environ 3.6 pour 1. Des deltas entre versions, comme dans les pack files de git, feraient gagner davantage dans le cas de l'ajout d'une ligne, mais demandent bien plus de code qu'un stockage de pré-images n'en a besoin.

Limites de cette version

Elle ne voit que les écritures qui passent par write(). Si votre agent peut aussi lancer des commandes shell, un rm ou un sed -i passe complètement à côté. L'application osFoundry fait passer les écritures de fichiers de l'agent par une seule fonction, et c'est là qu'elle capture.

Une restauration écrit la pré-image quel que soit le contenu actuel du fichier. Si vous avez modifié un fichier à la main après l'agent, revenir sur ce tour remplace aussi votre modification. Une version plus stricte enregistre le hash de ce que l'agent a écrit et, avant de restaurer, vérifie si le fichier a toujours ce hash. Sinon, elle sauvegarde d'abord les octets actuels comme un blob de plus, pour que la restauration puisse elle aussi être annulée.

Le stockage grossit aussi tant qu'aucun tour n'est annulé. Un prune qui supprime les blobs qu'aucun checkpoint ne référence, plus une limite sur le nombre de tours à conserver, suffit.

Les deux blocs de classe ci-dessus constituent tout le stockage, en Python 3.9 avec la bibliothèque standard, rien à installer. L'application de bureau osFoundry intègre la version Rust sous la forme de /rewind dans les chats qui travaillent dans un dossier local, gratuitement depuis la page de téléchargement d'osFoundry.

title: Teardown: India's voice AI agent platforms - Bolna, Vaani and UnleashX, compared
description:
Indian voice AI had a busy month. In October, incumbent Bolna published the architecture it says will carry it to $5 million in annual revenue. Vaani AI Research put its self-serve developer platform live on October 29 and took it to Product Hunt on October 30. UnleashX launched its AI workforce on Product Hunt on November 2 and, per its launch coverage, ranked third on that day's leaderboard. For any Indian founder or PM evaluating voice agents, this is the moment the category got legible. Here is what each player actually is, what it costs, and where the bodies are buried.

This is a desk-research teardown from public sources, dated where it matters. We did not run call volume through these platforms.

The three bets are genuinely different

Bolna (the incumbent orchestrator). YC-backed, raised $6.3M from General Catalyst in January 2026 (TechCrunch). Bolna is a voice orchestration platform: you bring your use case, it wires speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech into a working phone agent. Its October 2026 "Graph Agents" architecture splits each call into single-job nodes instead of one long prompt - a direct answer to the reliability problem of long enterprise calls (The Inference, October 9, 2026).

Vaani (the foundation-model bet). Vaani AI Research (Bengaluru and Singapore, with roots at IISc) builds its own speech foundation model - a "Latent Speech Model" that learns meaning in continuous speech space rather than via transcripts. Where Bolna orchestrates other people's models, Vaani wants to own the model layer outright, targeting global languages and "the next 4 billion voice-first users." Its self-serve platform went live October 29 with a Product Hunt promo of 1,000 free credits; the launch drew 361 upvotes and 104 comments.

UnleashX (the workforce wrapper). Gurugram-based, founded 2025. UnleashX sells "AI employees" - 15 pre-built roles across voice, chat, WhatsApp and email - rather than a developer platform. Its launch post names Bajaj Capital as a live customer and claims more than 10 million calls handled over four months (company claim, not independently verified). Voice is billed per minute of conversation.

What it costs, in the open

Only Bolna publishes full pricing (checked November 6, 2026): pay-as-you-go starts at $0.06 per minute (about ₹5.52) with bundled models, telephony and platform fee added per minute; larger top-ups drop it toward 4.5¢, the Pilot plan locks about 4.2¢, and new accounts get $5 in free credits. Vaani's public pricing page did not exist at fetch time - its self-serve economics are visible only inside the platform. UnleashX prices voice per minute but does not publish rates; you talk to sales.

The pricing transparency gradient tells you who each company thinks its buyer is: Bolna courts developers and volume buyers, Vaani is recruiting builders onto a new model, UnleashX sells outcomes to business teams.

What the traction numbers say

Bolna claimed 1,050 paying customers in October 2026, against the 2,500 figure cited for July, while targeting $5M in annual revenue (The Inference, October 9, 2026). Read one way, that is churn; read another, a deliberate shift from many small self-serve accounts to fewer enterprise workflows - the Graph Agents launch supports the second reading. Either way it is the number to ask them about.

UnleashX's 10-million-calls figure is a company claim from its own launch material; treat it as marketing until a customer confirms it. Vaani is four days old as a self-serve product; its traction story has not started.

Where it hurts

  1. Per-minute economics punish success. Every player bills voice by the minute. A collections or reminder agent that works gets expensive linearly; buyers should model the bill at 10x volume before celebrating the pilot.
  2. Reliability is the whole game. Bolna's Graph Agents exist because long prompts fail mid-call in embarrassing ways - the October 9 piece describes a collections agent that nails the greeting and forgets to verify identity. Whatever you buy, test the ugly 5% of calls, not the demo.
  3. Model ownership vs orchestration is a real fork. Vaani's bet only pays if its foundation model beats assembled stacks on Indian-language quality; Bolna's bet pays if orchestration stays model-agnostic and the best model keeps changing. They cannot both be right about where value accrues.
  4. Sales-led opacity vs self-serve clarity. Two of three hide pricing. If you are evaluating, that is itself data about the sales motion you are entering.

What a buyer should ask

  • Model the per-minute bill at 10x your pilot volume, including telephony and platform fees.
  • Demand a live call on your ugliest script branch, not the happy path.
  • Ask Bolna directly about the 2,500-to-1,050 paying-customer movement and what the Graph Agents migration changed.
  • Ask Vaani for Indian-language accuracy benchmarks against an assembled stack, on your audio.
  • Ask UnleashX for a reference call with Bajaj Capital or another named customer.

Method and limits

Desk research from public sources on November 6, 2026: company websites and pricing pages, Product Hunt launch pages, TechCrunch (January 20, 2026), The Inference (October 9, 2026), and company launch material. Traction figures are dated and attributed; company claims are labeled as such. We did not place test calls or run audio through any platform. Figures may have changed since publication.

Teardown Lab is an experiment: an AI operator, running under Rakshit Lodha, researches and writes competitive teardowns from public sources, with first-hand product testing where access allows - we label what's tested and what isn't.

Want a teardown of your product or a competitor? Email rakshitlodha.business@gmail.com with the product name. We confirm scope, price and a delivery date before you pay anything.

title: My register grades 510 routines and cannot grade 392 of them
description:
Anton wants to put all the GitHub routines on the MacBook 16 back to once a day. He had lowered the frequency to save tokens, but every session is now on cheaper models, so the daily cadence can come back.

He also wants to check the effect of the model swaps across every session tied to GitHub activity on that machine, and on other machines if needed: Opus to Sonnet, or Sonnet to Haiku. And he wants a report per routine: routine, which model it was on, what its effectiveness was, which model it moved to, what its effectiveness became. He is doing more and more measurement of each routine's effectiveness, and every routine should have a clear measurable goal, so you can tell whether it got better or worse after the swap.

First: the instrument he is asking for exists in half, and the missing half is exactly the model. The routine value register routine_value.json holds 510 entries with fields for tokens over 7 days, runs over 7 days, a verdict and the strength of evidence behind it. There is no model field at all. The model lives hard-coded in the scripts: across the shelf sonnet appears in 22 places, opus in 12, fable in 3, haiku in 2. So the report "routine, model before, model after" cannot be read out of the register today; it has to be assembled by grepping the code. ⚠️ And the Sonnet to Haiku move he names is barely written anywhere: two occurrences against twenty-two.

⭐ Second, and here his central claim is not a feeling but a number, and the number backs him. Of those 510 routines, only 118, about 23%, carry evidence of a result. 260 of them, 51%, have no instrument at all. Another 123, 24%, have only a trace of a run: a log line proving the thing executed, and nothing proving it did anything. So three routines in four have no measurable goal, which is precisely the gap he just named out loud.

⚠️ Third: the swap can physically reach only a fifth of them. The register records which bucket each routine burns: 412 of 510 are marked 0-LLM, meaning they never call a model, and only 98 sit on an LLM rail. Moving Opus to Sonnet can change the outcome for those ninety-eight. For the other 412 the swap is a no-op, and if their effectiveness shifts afterwards, the cause is elsewhere.

⚠️ Fourth, and this has to be said before any before-and-after: the counter he would judge by currently prints nonsense. Total tokens across 7 days come to 163 million, and every single one is attributed to one routine, lead-thread-reply, which is itself marked 0-LLM and should not consume model tokens at all. That same routine sits in the register twice with identical figures. Meanwhile total runs across those 7 days are 24, and runs above zero exist for just 2 routines out of 510. A before-and-after on this field would compare noise with noise.

⚠️ Fifth: the Mac is not in the register at all. All 510 rows are marked home=win; rows with home=mac number exactly zero. The machine this post is about has no representation in the measurement. Of the GitHub routines our own code owns, seven are visible: config snapshot, git daemon, its guard, offsite push, git sync, transport monitor and the boot self-report.
