 "description": "Queue a bounded goal for an agent, team, or loop session where this assistant is an invited runner. The osFoundry runtime executes the task when available.",
 "required": ["session_type","session_id","goal","idempotency_key"],
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "openWorldHint": false, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:run"]}]}

둘 다 결국 세션이 일을 하게 만든다. 이 글에서는 왜 하나로 안 합쳤는지, 각각 어떤 제한이 걸려 있는지 보고, 클라이언트 쪽을 Python으로 다시 만들어서 그 제한을 라이브 스키마에 직접 대 봤다.

두 호출을 가르는 건 뭘까

누가, 언제 OK를 하느냐다.

핸드오프는 그 자리에서 사람한테 묻는다. 오너한테 "Codex CLI requests a handoff" 알림이 가고, 세션의 Handoffs 탭 "Outside assistant requests"에 올라온다. 보이는 건 goal, 접혀 있는 "Context and expected output", 그리고 "Up to N rounds on your agent runtime" 한 줄이다. 누가 Accept and run을 누르기 전까지 큐에는 아무것도 안 들어간다. 웹 클라이언트는 /agent-sessions/{id}/external-handoffs/{handoff_id}/decision에 {decision: "accept"}를 POST하고, 토스트로 "Handoff accepted and run queued"가 뜬다. 핸드오프 행은 pending에서 accepted, declined, cancelled 중 하나로 넘어간다.

run은 승인이 이미 끝나 있다. 오너가 Connected 탭에서 연결에 Runner 자리를 준 순간이 OK다. 거기 설명문은 이렇다. "Invite it to a session as Contributor to post notes and propose handoffs, or Runner to also request runs. A handoff still needs the session owner's approval." 로그인 화면에서도 run 스코프는 "Run sessions where you grant a runner role"로 나온다.

needs_approval 플래그 하나 달린 툴로 합쳤다면, 사람한테 물을지 말지를 호출하는 쪽이 정하게 된다. 툴을 둘로 쪼개면 그 결정이 오너 쪽, 그것도 호출자가 손댈 수 없는 두 군데로 간다. OAuth 스코프(osfoundry:write냐 osfoundry:run이냐)와 자리(Contributor냐 Runner냐)다. Codex 설정의 scopes에서 osfoundry:run을 빼 두면 Runner 자리가 있어도 run을 못 띄운다.

어노테이션도 같은 선으로 갈린다. propose_session_handoff는 결과가 호출 밖의 사람한테 닿으니까 openWorldHint: true. request_session_run은 미리 동의한 세션의 큐만 건드리니까 openWorldHint: false. 둘 다 destructiveHint: true라서 Codex를 default_tools_approval_mode = "writes"로 돌리면 둘 다 실행 전에 확인을 받는다.

핸드오프만 컨텍스트 요약이 필수인 이유

뭔가 돌기 전에 사람이 읽기 때문이다. context_summary와 requested_output은 핸드오프에선 필수고 run에는 아예 없다. 오너는 자기 세션 런타임을 여기에 쓸지 말지 정해야 하는데, "export 고쳐줘"만으로는 못 정한다. Runner는 그 신뢰를 이미 받았으니 run은 goal만 받는다.

길이 제한도 다르다. 핸드오프의 goal은 5,000자, 컨텍스트 5,000자, 원하는 결과물 1,000자까지. run의 goal은 10,000자까지 된다. run엔 다른 칸이 없으니 실제로는 goal에 컨텍스트까지 같이 쓰게 된다.

Codex는 뭘 다시 읽을 수 있나

세션이 가진 것보다 적다.

  • read_session_task_result: "the status and attributed runtime result for one task started by this connection". 다른 연결의 task id를 넣어도 소용없다.
  • read_session_mail: "notes addressed to this connection and notes it posted". 페이지당 1~20개, 오래된 건 before_id로 넘긴다. "Internal agent analysis is excluded."
  • read_session_state: 참여한 세션의 현재 상태와 최근 태스크.
  • post_session_note: 이름이 붙은 노트를 남긴다. 에이전트는 "the returned external sender slug"로 답장할 수 있다. "does not trigger an automatic run"이라서 노트로 오너의 클릭을 우회할 수는 없다.

팀 세션에서는 이 노트가 Team mail에 연결의 표시 이름과 "outside assistant" 라벨을 달고 올라온다.

다시 만들어 보기

이 Mac엔 codex 바이너리가 없어서 handoff_sim.py(약 220줄)가 클라이언트 역할을 한다. 하는 일은 세 가지다.

  1. 토큰 없이 라이브 서버에 initialize, tools/list, tools/call을 각각 15번 보내고 툴 목록을 저장한다.
  2. 인자 케이스 12개를 라이브 inputSchema에 jsonschema(Draft 2020-12)로 검증한다. 제한값은 추측하지 않는다.
  3. 자리, 스코프, 오너의 결정, 멱등성을 작은 인메모리 모델로 돌린다. osFoundry 서버 코드는 공개돼 있지 않아서, 이 부분은 툴 설명과 핸드오프를 보여 주는 웹 클라이언트를 보고 재구성한 거다. 응답은 모델의 것이지 서버의 것이 아니다. 
$ uv run --with tiktoken --with jsonschema python3 handoff_sim.py

와이어 

initialize             HTTP 200  median  566.3  p90  799.0
tools/list             HTTP 200  median  559.7  p90  937.7
tools/call (no token)  HTTP 401  median  482.6  p90  677.0

단위는 밀리초. 일본에 있는 이 Mac에서 CloudFront KIX 엣지를 거쳐 잰 거라 서버보다는 경로 숫자에 가깝다. 볼 건 모양이다. 툴 탐색은 공짜고 Codex 켤 때마다 돌려도 부담이 없다. 첫 진짜 호출은 401 왕복 한 번이 들고, 그 401이 resource_metadata를 실어 온다. Codex는 따로 알려 주지 않아도 이걸로 OAuth 서버를 찾는다.

세션 툴 7개는 전체 목록 10,197토큰 중 1,152토큰(11.3%)이었다. cl100k_base로 센 거라 Codex 토크나이저 기준으로는 대략적인 값이다. enabled_tools에 이 7개만 넣으면 프롬프트가 작아진다.

제한값

툴 스코프 필수 제한
propose_session_handoff write 6 goal 5,000, context 5,000, output 1,000, max_rounds 1–10
cancel_session_handoff write 1 handoff_id만
request_session_run run 4 goal 10,000, max_rounds 1–10
read_session_state read 2 없음
read_session_task_result read 3 없음
read_session_mail read 2 limit 1–20
post_session_note write 5 subject 200, body 10,000

라이브 스키마에 12케이스를 대 본 결과다.

propose_session_handoff   6,000-char goal        REJECT maxLength: goal
request_session_run       6,000-char goal        ok
propose_session_handoff   no context_summary     REJECT required
propose_session_handoff   max_rounds omitted     ok
request_session_run       max_rounds 0           REJECT minimum: max_rounds
request_session_run       max_rounds 11          REJECT maximum: max_rounds
request_session_run       no idempotency_key     REJECT required
request_session_run       session_type 'room'    REJECT enum: session_type
request_session_run       extra field 'model'    REJECT additionalProperties
read_session_mail         limit 21               REJECT maximum: limit
post_session_note         201-char subject       REJECT maxLength: subject
cancel_session_handoff    only handoff_id        ok

두 개는 다시 볼 만하다. 같은 6,000자 goal이 run에선 통과하고 핸드오프에선 너무 길다. 긴 프롬프트 하나 만들어서 쓸 수 있는 툴에 아무거나 던지는 클라이언트는 여기서 삽질한다. 그리고 additionalProperties: false가 model 필드를 막는다. 호출자는 세션 모델을 고를 수 없고, 세션은 자기 설정대로 돈다.

max_rounds는 둘 다 생략할 수 있다. 기본값이 스키마에 안 나와 있으니 횟수가 중요하면 명시해서 보내는 게 낫다.

자리, 취소, 승인 (모델) 

tool                      observer contributor runner
propose_session_handoff   -        yes         yes
cancel_session_handoff    -        yes         yes
request_session_run       -        -           yes
read_session_state        yes      yes         yes
read_session_task_result  yes      yes         yes
read_session_mail         yes      yes         yes
post_session_note         -        yes         yes
runner seat, token without osfoundry:run -> {'error': 'token lacks osfoundry:run'}

cancel while pending -> {'status': 'cancelled'}
owner clicks Accept after cancel -> cancelled
owner accepts -> accepted | cancel after -> {'error': 'already accepted'}
another connection reads that task -> {'error': 'not a task started by this connection'}

표는 Connected 탭 설명문을 그대로 표로 옮긴 거다. 재밌는 건 취소 창이다. cancel_session_handoff는 "before its owner accepts it"에만 먹히니까, 먼저 일어난 쪽이 이긴다. run이 큐에 들어간 뒤엔 거두는 게 더 이상 호출자 몫이 아니다. 취소가 handoff_id만 받는 것도 그래서다. 넘길 상태가 없고, 닫을 건 대기 중인 행 하나뿐이다.

응답이 사라질 때

쓰기 툴은 전부 idempotency_key가 필수다. 이게 뭘 막는지 보려고 모델에서 request_session_run을 1,000번 보내고, 응답의 20%를 버리고(seed 7), 클라이언트가 같은 키로 최대 3번 재시도하게 했다.

server honours idempotency_key=True  calls sent 1276  tasks queued 1000  duplicates 0
server honours idempotency_key=False calls sent 1276  tasks queued 1276  duplicates 276

남의 런타임에서 run이 276번 더 도는 거다. 필수 키는 바로 이 경우 때문에 있다. 타임아웃 나서 재시도하는 클라이언트라면 누구나 밟을 수 있고, 이미 시작된 run은 두 번 필요 없다. 선택이 아니라 필수라서 빼먹는 클라이언트가 나올 수 없다.

스크립트 전체는 Apple M1에서 실시간 26.4초 걸렸다. 거의 다 네트워크 호출 45번이고 user CPU 시간은 0.37초였다.

직접 붙인다면

  • "사람한테 묻기"와 "미리 받은 허락으로 움직이기"를 스코프가 다른 두 툴로 나눈다. 오너의 선택은 호출자가 정하는 인자가 아니라 토큰과 자리에 둔다.
  • 사람이 판단할 때 쓰는 필드(context_summary, requested_output)는 제안 쪽에만 필수로 두고, run의 goal보다 제한을 빡빡하게 잡는다.
  • 호출자가 취소할 수 있는 건 대기 중일 때뿐이다. 승인 후에 멈추는 건 오너 일이다.
  • 다시 읽기는 그 연결이 시작한 것, 그 연결 앞으로 온 것으로 좁힌다. 세션 내부 분석은 빼 둔다.
  • 쓰기는 전부 idempotency_key 필수로 하고, 중복이면 첫 결과를 돌려준다.
  • 스키마는 additionalProperties: false로 닫아서, 세션이 고르지 않은 모델이나 툴 목록을 호출자가 끼워 넣지 못하게 한다.

osFoundry 에이전트끼리 단계 사이에 일을 넘기는 방식은 핸드오프 페이지에 있다. 밑에 깔린 프로토콜은 MCP 용어 설명을 보면 된다.

title: Claude Message Threads API: Agent Loops in TypeScript
description:
The Claude message threads API solves a problem that anyone who has built an agent loop knows well: every tool call makes the request bigger. The Messages API is stateless, so each step sends the entire conversation again, including the system prompt and the tool definitions. After twenty steps, a hefty chunk of JSON crosses the wire every time just so Claude can read one new line.

Since November 2, 2026, there is a beta for this. The API holds on to the conversation for a short while, and you only send the new messages. I am mostly interested in it for agents that take many small tool steps. At the same time, the feature has a trap: if you do not build the way back for expired threads from day one, your application simply fails after a five-minute pause.

In short

With message threads, the Claude API keeps a conversation for up to five minutes after the last request, so follow-up requests only contain the new messages. Requests get smaller and the first token arrives sooner, but prices stay the same. The biggest pitfall: a thread can disappear at any time, so you need your own copy of the conversation and a replay path.

What you will learn in this article

  • How create, continue and replay work together in message threads
  • When threads pay off and when to skip them (data retention, Bedrock)
  • A tested TypeScript class that uses threads with automatic replay
  • An agent loop with a tool that only sends tool results
  • Which fields must not change inside a thread and common error codes

What is the Claude message threads API?

Normally the Messages API forgets everything after each response. That is deliberate and has advantages: you keep full control over the history, you can shorten or rewrite messages, and you do not depend on state on the server. The price is that every request carries the entire context.

A thread flips this for a moment. On the first request you send everything as usual and add "thread": {"type": "create"}. The API keeps the conversation together with Claude's answer and files it under that answer's ID. On the next step you only send the new messages and point to the last reply with previous_message_id. According to Anthropic, this lowers the time to first token (the time until the first token of the reply arrives) and keeps it steadier in long conversations.

Create, continue and replay

There are three situations you need to know:

  • Create: the first request with the full conversation, system and tools.
  • Continue: a follow-up request with the new messages and the ID of the previous reply. You leave out system and tools.
  • Replay: the thread is gone. You send the full conversation from your own copy again as a create and carry on with the new ID.

Plan for the third case, because it is part of the design. A thread expires five minutes after the last request and is deleted no later than one hour after its last use. Anthropic explicitly describes threads as “best-effort”, so there is no guarantee. Your application remains the source of truth.

🎬 Create, continue and replay with Claude message threads – this animated diagram only runs on my site: watch it on sascha-ms.de

When does the Claude message threads API pay off?

Threads help most when a conversation has many short rounds with small pauses in between. A typical case is an agent loop: Claude calls a tool, your code returns the result, Claude calls the next tool. Each round adds only a few blocks, and the context before it stays the same.

Schematic: without a thread every request grows with the history, with a thread only the new part is sent.

According to the documentation, prices and rate limits do not change. So threads save you transfer volume and latency, while token costs stay the same. For costs, prompt caching remains the tool of choice; more on that below.

Situation Use threads? Why
Agent loop with many tool steps Yes Many rounds in quick succession, growing context
Chat where people type Sometimes Pauses over five minutes lead to a replay
Single request without follow-ups No There is nothing to continue
Message Batches or token counting No Both are rejected with thread
Data with ZDR or HIPAA requirements No Threads are neither ZDR nor HIPAA eligible
Claude via Amazon Bedrock No Bedrock is not listed under availability

The data retention point deserves a second look. ZDR stands for zero data retention, the promise that requests are not stored. According to Anthropic, threads are held encrypted in memory, never written to durable storage, and deleted within one hour at the latest. That is fine for many applications. If your company has ZDR in its contract, though, check with the people responsible first.

The beta is available on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) and Microsoft Foundry. If you use Claude via Amazon Bedrock, you will have to do without it for now. For agents on Bedrock, a clean token budget for AI agents is the better place to start.

Step by step: Claude message threads in TypeScript

Now I will build a small class that uses threads and repairs itself when a thread disappears. On top of that comes an agent loop with a tool for a fictional bike rental, the “Lindenhof Bike Station”. I deliberately use direct HTTP calls via fetch instead of the SDK, so you can see exactly what goes over the wire.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 22 or newer (tested with 22.23) and npm
  • TypeScript 7 (tested with 7.0.2)
  • For the real run, a Claude API key in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  • The tests run without a key and without network access

The API version in the header is 2026-10-21. I described what changed with this version, such as the removal of temperature, in Claude API 2026-10-21: migrating to the new SDK.

Step 1: Create the project 

mkdir claude-message-threads && cd claude-message-threads
mkdir src test
npm init -y
npm install --save-dev typescript@^7.0.2 @types/node@^24

Then replace the package.json and create the tsconfig.json:

{
  "name": "claude-message-threads",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "tsc -p tsconfig.json",
    "test": "npm run build && node --test dist/test/*.test.js",
    "start": "npm run build && node dist/src/main.js"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@types/node": "^24.0.0",
    "typescript": "^7.0.2"
  }
}

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": ".",
    "strict": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "types": ["node"]
  },
  "include": ["src", "test"]
}

Step 2: The ThreadedConversation class

The core keeps its own copy of the conversation and decides on every call whether to create, continue or replay a thread. Read the code once calmly; the comments explain the places where the documentation sets clear rules.

// src/threaded-conversation.ts
// Keeps a conversation with Claude in a message thread (beta) and replays it when needed.

export type Role = 'user' | 'assistant';
export type ContentBlock = { type: string; [key: string]: unknown };
export interface Message {
  role: Role;
  content: string | ContentBlock[];
}
export interface ToolDefinition {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  input_schema: Record<string, unknown>;
}
export interface ClaudeResponse {
  id: string;
  role: 'assistant';
  content: ContentBlock[];
  stop_reason: string | null;
  usage?: Record<string, unknown>;
}

export type RequestKind = 'create' | 'continue' | 'replay' | 'unthreaded';

export interface ThreadOptions {
  apiKey: string;
  model: string;
  maxTokens: number;
  system?: string;
  tools?: ToolDefinition[];
  baseUrl?: string;
  fetchFn?: typeof fetch;
  onRequest?: (kind: RequestKind, messagesSent: number) => void;
}

const API_VERSION = '2026-10-21';
const THREADS_BETA = 'message-threads-2026-08-12';

export class ClaudeApiError extends Error {
  constructor(
    readonly status: number,
    readonly errorCode: string | undefined,
    message: string,
    readonly unsupported: string[] = [],
  ) {
    super(message);
    this.name = 'ClaudeApiError';
  }
}

// These errors mean the thread is gone or cannot be continued: replay it.
const REPLAY_CODES = new Set([
  'thread_not_found',
  'thread_already_continued',
  'thread_continue_in_flight',
]);

export class ThreadedConversation {
  private readonly history: Message[] = [];
  private previousId: string | undefined;
  private threadsDisabled = false;
  private readonly fetchFn: typeof fetch;

  constructor(private readonly options: ThreadOptions) {
    this.fetchFn = options.fetchFn ?? fetch;
  }

  /** Your own complete copy of the conversation: the source of truth. */
  get messages(): readonly Message[] {
    return this.history;
  }

  /** Sends new messages. An empty array continues a paused response (pause_turn). */
  async send(newMessages: Message[]): Promise<ClaudeResponse> {
    this.history.push(...newMessages);
    let response: ClaudeResponse;
    try {
      response = await this.request(newMessages);
    } catch (error) {
      // Failed request: roll the copy back to the last good state.
      this.history.splice(this.history.length - newMessages.length, newMessages.length);
      throw error;
    }

    if (response.stop_reason === 'refusal') {
      // Do not continue a refused turn: drop it from the copy, the next call starts over.
      this.history.splice(this.history.length - newMessages.length, newMessages.length);
      this.previousId = undefined;
      return response;
    }

    this.appendAssistant(response.content);
    this.previousId = this.threadsDisabled ? undefined : response.id;
    return response;
  }

  private async request(newMessages: Message[]): Promise<ClaudeResponse> {
    if (this.threadsDisabled) {
      return this.post('unthreaded', this.history);
    }
    if (!this.previousId) {
      return this.createOrFallBack('create');
    }
    try {
      return await this.post('continue', newMessages);
    } catch (error) {
      if (error instanceof ClaudeApiError && error.errorCode && REPLAY_CODES.has(error.errorCode)) {
        return this.createOrFallBack('replay');
      }
      throw error;
    }
  }

  private async createOrFallBack(kind: 'create' | 'replay'): Promise<ClaudeResponse> {
    try {
      return await this.post(kind, this.history);
    } catch (error) {
      const tooBig = kind === 'replay' && error instanceof ClaudeApiError && error.errorCode === 'thread_not_found';
      const unsupported = error instanceof ClaudeApiError && error.errorCode === 'thread_unsupported_request';
      if (tooBig || unsupported) {
        // Threads speed things up but are optional: carry on without a thread.
        this.threadsDisabled = true;
        return this.post('unthreaded', this.history);
      }
      throw error;
    }
  }

  private appendAssistant(content: ContentBlock[]): void {
    const last = this.history.at(-1);
    if (last?.role === 'assistant' && Array.isArray(last.content)) {
      // Continuation after pause_turn: append to the existing reply.
      last.content.push(...content);
      return;
    }
    this.history.push({ role: 'assistant', content: [...content] });
  }

  private buildBody(kind: RequestKind, messages: readonly Message[]): Record<string, unknown> {
    const { model, maxTokens, system, tools } = this.options;
    const body: Record<string, unknown> = {
      model,
      max_tokens: maxTokens,
      cache_control: { type: 'ephemeral' },
      messages,
    };
    if (kind !== 'continue') {
      if (system) body.system = system;
      if (tools?.length) body.tools = tools;
    }
    if (kind === 'create' || kind === 'replay') {
      body.thread = { type: 'create' };
    }
    if (kind === 'continue') {
      body.thread = { type: 'continue', previous_message_id: this.previousId };
    }
    return body;
  }

  private async post(kind: RequestKind, messages: readonly Message[]): Promise<ClaudeResponse> {
    this.options.onRequest?.(kind, messages.length);
    const headers: Record<string, string> = {
      'content-type': 'application/json',
      'x-api-key': this.options.apiKey,
      'anthropic-version': API_VERSION,
    };
    if (kind !== 'unthreaded') headers['anthropic-beta'] = THREADS_BETA;

    const res = await this.fetchFn(`${this.options.baseUrl ?? 'https://api.anthropic.com'}/v1/messages`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers,
      body: JSON.stringify(this.buildBody(kind, messages)),
    });
    const json = (await res.json()) as Record<string, any>;
    if (!res.ok) {
      const err = json?.error ?? {};
      throw new ClaudeApiError(res.status, err.details?.error_code, err.message ?? `HTTP ${res.status}`, err.details?.unsupported ?? []);
    }
    return json as ClaudeResponse;
  }
}

Three decisions are built in. First, send() adds the new messages to its own copy and removes them again if the request fails. Second, only an error code from error.details.error_code triggers a replay. A normal 404 caused by a wrong model name therefore does not end up in an endless loop. Third, the class switches to requests without a thread if recreating fails as well or if the organization does not support threads. The application gets a little slower then, but it keeps working.

Step 3: Agent loop with a tool

Now for the tool. The bike rental has two stations and three bike types; for simplicity the data lives in the code.

// src/bike-tools.ts
// Fictional bike rental "Lindenhof Bike Station" as an example tool.
import type { ToolDefinition } from './threaded-conversation.js';
import type { ToolHandler } from './agent-loop.js';

const STOCK: Record<string, Record<string, number>> = {
  Lindenhof: { citybike: 4, ebike: 1, cargo: 0 },
  Hafen: { citybike: 2, ebike: 3, cargo: 1 },
};

export const bikeTools: ToolDefinition[] = [
  {
    name: 'find_available_bikes',
    description: 'Returns the available bikes at a station, optionally filtered by type.',
    input_schema: {
      type: 'object',
      properties: {
        station: { type: 'string', enum: Object.keys(STOCK) },
        type: { type: 'string', enum: ['citybike', 'ebike', 'cargo'] },
      },
      required: ['station'],
    },
  },
];

export const bikeHandlers: Record<string, ToolHandler> = {
  async find_available_bikes(input) {
    const station = STOCK[String(input.station)];
    if (!station) return { error: 'Unknown station' };
    const type = input.type ? String(input.type) : undefined;
    return type ? { [type]: station[type] ?? 0 } : station;
  },
};

The loop itself is short. Pay attention to the last line in the loop body: while a thread is running, only a single message with the tool results goes out there.

// src/agent-loop.ts
// A lean agent loop: Claude calls tools until the answer is ready.
import type { ContentBlock, ThreadedConversation } from './threaded-conversation.js';

export type ToolHandler = (input: Record<string, unknown>) => Promise<unknown>;

export async function runAgent(
  conversation: ThreadedConversation,
  userText: string,
  handlers: Record<string, ToolHandler>,
  maxSteps = 10,
): Promise<string> {
  let response = await conversation.send([{ role: 'user', content: userText }]);

  for (let step = 0; step < maxSteps; step++) {
    if (response.stop_reason === 'pause_turn') {
      // A server tool paused: continue without a new message.
      response = await conversation.send([]);
      continue;
    }
    if (response.stop_reason !== 'tool_use') {
      return textOf(response.content);
    }

    const results: ContentBlock[] = [];
    for (const block of response.content.filter((b) => b.type === 'tool_use')) {
      const handler = handlers[String(block.name)];
      const output = handler
        ? await handler(block.input as Record<string, unknown>)
        : { error: `Unknown tool: ${String(block.name)}` };
      results.push({ type: 'tool_result', tool_use_id: block.id, content: JSON.stringify(output) });
    }
    // With a thread, only these results go over the wire, not the whole conversation.
    response = await conversation.send([{ role: 'user', content: results }]);
  }
  throw new Error(`Agent stopped after ${maxSteps} steps without a result`);
}

function textOf(content: ContentBlock[]): string {
  return content
    .filter((b) => b.type === 'text')
    .map((b) => String(b.text))
    .join('\n');
}

The special case pause_turn shows up with server-side tools such as web search. The documentation says to continue from the paused reply with an empty messages array and not to send a new user message. That is exactly what send([]) does.

Step 4: Test without an API key

The tests replace fetch with a function that returns prepared replies and records every request. This lets you check what is really sent.

// test/threaded-conversation.test.ts
// Checks create, continue and replay with a fake fetch function, without real API calls.
import { test } from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import { ClaudeApiError, ThreadedConversation } from '../src/threaded-conversation.js';
import { runAgent } from '../src/agent-loop.js';
import { bikeHandlers, bikeTools } from '../src/bike-tools.js';

type Reply = { status: number; body: unknown };

function fakeFetch(replies: Reply[]) {
  const calls: { headers: Record<string, string>; body: any }[] = [];
  const fn = (async (_url: string, init: RequestInit) => {
    calls.push({ headers: init.headers as Record<string, string>, body: JSON.parse(String(init.body)) });
    const reply = replies.shift();
    if (!reply) throw new Error('No prepared reply left');
    return new Response(JSON.stringify(reply.body), { status: reply.status });
  }) as unknown as typeof fetch;
  return { fn, calls };
}

const ok = (id: string, text: string, stop = 'end_turn'): Reply => ({
  status: 200,
  body: { id, role: 'assistant', content: [{ type: 'text', text }], stop_reason: stop },
});
const threadError = (status: number, code: string): Reply => ({
  status,
  body: { type: 'error', error: { type: 'x', message: code, details: { error_code: code } } },
});

function conversation(fn: typeof fetch) {
  return new ThreadedConversation({
    apiKey: 'test',
    model: 'claude-opus-5-5',
    maxTokens: 256,
    system: 'Answer briefly.',
    tools: bikeTools,
    fetchFn: fn,
  });
}

test('first call creates the thread with system and tools', async () => {
  const { fn, calls } = fakeFetch([ok('msg_1', 'Hello!')]);
  await conversation(fn).send([{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }]);
  assert.deepEqual(calls[0].body.thread, { type: 'create' });
  assert.equal(calls[0].body.system, 'Answer briefly.');
  assert.equal(calls[0].headers['anthropic-beta'], 'message-threads-2026-08-12');
});

test('follow-up call sends only the new message and the previous ID', async () => {
  const { fn, calls } = fakeFetch([ok('msg_1', 'Hello!'), ok('msg_2', 'Two hours.')]);
  const c = conversation(fn);
  await c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }]);
  await c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'How long can I rent?' }]);
  assert.deepEqual(calls[1].body.thread, { type: 'continue', previous_message_id: 'msg_1' });
  assert.equal(calls[1].body.messages.length, 1);
  assert.equal('system' in calls[1].body, false);
  assert.equal('tools' in calls[1].body, false);
  assert.equal(c.messages.length, 4);
});

test('expired thread is recreated with the full history', async () => {
  const { fn, calls } = fakeFetch([
    ok('msg_1', 'Hello!'),
    threadError(404, 'thread_not_found'),
    ok('msg_3', 'Two hours.'),
  ]);
  const c = conversation(fn);
  await c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }]);
  const res = await c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'How long can I rent?' }]);
  assert.equal(res.id, 'msg_3');
  assert.deepEqual(calls[2].body.thread, { type: 'create' });
  assert.equal(calls[2].body.messages.length, 3);
  assert.equal(calls[2].body.system, 'Answer briefly.');
});

test('if recreating fails too, it continues without a thread', async () => {
  const { fn, calls } = fakeFetch([
    ok('msg_1', 'Hello!'),
    threadError(404, 'thread_not_found'),
    threadError(404, 'thread_not_found'),
    ok('msg_4', 'Two hours.'),
  ]);
  const c = conversation(fn);
  await c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }]);
  await c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'How long?' }]);
  assert.equal('thread' in calls[3].body, false);
  assert.equal(calls[3].headers['anthropic-beta'], undefined);
});

test('a different 404 (such as a wrong model) is not swallowed', async () => {
  const { fn } = fakeFetch([
    ok('msg_1', 'Hello!'),
    { status: 404, body: { type: 'error', error: { type: 'not_found_error', message: 'model: x' } } },
  ]);
  const c = conversation(fn);
  await c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'Hi' }]);
  await assert.rejects(c.send([{ role: 'user', content: 'And?' }]), ClaudeApiError);
  assert.equal(c.messages.length, 2);
});

test('agent loop sends tool results as the only new message', async () => {
  const { fn, calls } = fakeFetch([
    {
      status: 200,
      body: {
        id: 'msg_1',
        role: 'assistant',
        stop_reason: 'tool_use',
        content: [{ type: 'tool_use', id: 'tu_1', name: 'find_available_bikes', input: { station: 'Hafen', type: 'cargo' } }],
      },
    },
    ok('msg_2', 'There is a free cargo bike at Hafen.'),
  ]);
  const answer = await runAgent(conversation(fn), 'Free cargo bike?', bikeHandlers);
  assert.equal(answer, 'There is a free cargo bike at Hafen.');
  const sent = calls[1].body.messages;
  assert.equal(sent.length, 1);
  assert.equal(sent[0].content[0].type, 'tool_result');
  assert.equal(sent[0].content[0].content, '{"cargo":1}');
});

npm test

Expected result (shortened):

✔ first call creates the thread with system and tools
✔ follow-up call sends only the new message and the previous ID
✔ expired thread is recreated with the full history
✔ if recreating fails too, it continues without a thread
✔ a different 404 (such as a wrong model) is not swallowed
✔ agent loop sends tool results as the only new message
ℹ tests 6
ℹ pass 6
ℹ fail 0

Step 5: Run it against the real API

Finally, a small start script. For every request it prints whether a thread was created, continued or replayed.

// src/main.ts
// Runs the agent loop against the real Claude API (requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY).
import { ThreadedConversation } from './threaded-conversation.js';
import { runAgent } from './agent-loop.js';
import { bikeHandlers, bikeTools } from './bike-tools.js';

const apiKey = process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) {
  console.error('Please set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.');
  process.exit(1);
}

const conversation = new ThreadedConversation({
  apiKey,
  model: process.env.CLAUDE_MODEL ?? 'claude-opus-5-5',
  maxTokens: 1024,
  system: 'You are the booking assistant of the Lindenhof Bike Station. Keep answers short.',
  tools: bikeTools,
  onRequest: (kind, sent) => console.log(`→ ${kind} (${sent} message(s) sent)`),
});

const answer = await runAgent(
  conversation,
  'Is there a free cargo bike at Hafen or at Lindenhof right now?',
  bikeHandlers,
);
console.log(answer);
console.log(`Own copy: ${conversation.messages.length} messages`);

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-key"
npm start

In a typical run you first see → create (1 message(s) sent) and then → continue (1 message(s) sent) for each tool result. The exact answer depends on the model.

Which fields stay fixed in a thread

A thread remembers more than the messages. It also stores a fingerprint of certain settings. If you change one of these fields in the middle of a thread, the API replies with HTTP 400 and the code thread_fingerprint_mismatch.

Group Fields Rule
Create only system, tools Leave them out on continue, do not send them as null either
Fixed model, tool_choice, thinking, mcp_servers, context_management, output_config, top-level cache_control, beta header Identical on every request
Free max_tokens, stop_sequences, stream, metadata, service_tier May change per round

If you want to change a fixed field, start a new thread. With the class above, that happens when you create a new instance with the existing history. There is one exception for mcp_servers and container: you have to send both on every request because the API stores neither MCP URLs nor tokens.

Combining prompt caching with threads

Threads do not cache automatically. If you want to save money, you set prompt caching yourself as usual. The simplest option is a top-level cache_control, as in the class above. Each round then reads the previous context from the cache and only writes the new round.

There are two rules you should know. A thread request allows at most four cache breakpoints, including the top-level cache_control. In addition, breakpoints you set on system or tools in the create request count again on every continue. So if you already have two breakpoints in your system prompt, you have little room left. When replaying, the documentation says to remove earlier breakpoints from message blocks before sending the conversation again.

Common mistakes and how to avoid them

Sending old messages on continue

The API does not deduplicate. If you send the whole history on continue, messages end up in the thread twice or the request fails. That is why the class above only sends the newMessages array on continue.

Continuing too early while streaming

When streaming, the reply ID already arrives in the message_start event. You may only continue after message_stop, otherwise you get a 404. If a stream breaks off earlier, send the same continue request again. If that returns thread_already_continued or thread_continue_in_flight, a replay helps. The documentation stresses that a replay is always safe.

Carrying on after a refusal

If a reply ends with stop_reason: "refusal", do not continue the thread. Start over, without the refused turn or with a rephrased question. The class therefore removes the turn from its own copy and creates a new thread on the next call.

Expecting compaction inside a thread

Threads are append-only, so they only grow. You cannot push a summary of older rounds into a running thread. If your agent needs to condense its context, condense it into a summary on your side and open a fresh thread from that summary. “Compaction on demand” is not supported with threads either.

Switching the API key

A thread belongs to the organization, the workspace and the key that created it. If your application rotates between several keys, for example to spread load, every switch ends in a replay. Use one fixed key per conversation.

My take

I like Claude message threads because the feature is built honestly. Anthropic promises a short-lived accelerator with clear rules and no permanent conversation store. That fits the way I would build agents anyway: the state belongs to the application, and the service may only cache it.

I see two things critically. One is the added complexity. A replay path that rarely runs is a path that will break one day without anyone noticing. That is why I would cover it with tests that force exactly this case, as in the example. The other is data protection. For many teams it is no problem that threads are not ZDR eligible, but it should be a conscious decision and not get lost in the fine print.

For chats with people, I would not introduce threads first. Whoever goes to get a coffee breaks the five minutes, and then the replay pays back the savings. Agents that call tools every few seconds are a different story. That is where the gain is largest and the risk is smallest.

FAQ

How long does a Claude message thread last?

A thread expires five minutes after the last request. Each stored reply restarts the five minutes. The API deletes it no later than one hour after its last use.

Are message threads cheaper than normal requests?

No. According to Anthropic, prices and rate limits do not change. You save transfer volume and get the first token sooner; you still lower costs with prompt caching.

Do message threads work with Amazon Bedrock?

The documentation does not list Bedrock as a platform. The beta is available on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) and Microsoft Foundry.

Can I read or delete a thread?

No, there is no API for that. That is why your own copy of the conversation is mandatory: it is the only way to replay an expired thread.

Your next step

Take your existing agent loop and count how many messages go out per request. If the number grows with every step and the steps follow each other quickly, try the class from this article in a test environment and write the test for the replay case first. I am curious: where would you use threads, and where does the missing ZDR status hold you back?

Sources

  • Claude Docs: Message threads (beta)
  • Claude Docs: Release notes (entry from November 2, 2026)
  • Claude Docs: Prompt caching
  • Claude Docs: Streaming
  • Node.js: Test runner

title: A hard daily cap on your AI agents’ API spend
description:
Every so often someone posts about leaving an agent running overnight and waking up to a surprising API bill. An agent stuck in a loop will keep calling the API until something stops it.

I didn't want that to happen to me, so I added a daily API budget to Saifuban, the spending guard for agents I've been building.

https://ut181749ut.github.io/saifuban/?src=devto

How it works

You store your provider API key in Saifuban and get a proxy key (sbk_...) back. The agent only ever sees the proxy key.

Requests go through Saifuban to the real API. Saifuban records the cost from the usage each response reports, and once the agent's spend for the day reaches its budget, it stops forwarding requests and returns an error instead:

403 [Saifuban] Over daily budget ($10.00)

The budget resets the next day.

Supported providers

  • OpenAI
  • Anthropic
  • Google (Gemini)
  • OpenRouter

OpenRouter reports the actual cost, so that's the most accurate. For the other three, the cost is calculated from token counts and the price table. Streaming responses are metered too.

Setup

  1. Open the site, press Start, and create an agent
  2. In Settings, store the API key for the provider you use
  3. Put the proxy base URL and the proxy key into your agent's config

For Claude Code, that's two environment variables:

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="https://zrphnuvrsldcycxtdftv.supabase.co/functions/v1/saifuban-proxy/anthropic"
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sbk_..."

Tools built on the OpenAI SDK work the same way with OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY.

Budgets are per agent, so a research agent can get $1/day and a coding agent $10/day.

Things to know

The budget check happens before each request. Requests that are already in flight when the budget is reached still go through, so the day can end slightly over budget, by at most those requests.

You are also handing your real API key to a third party. It's kept in an encrypted vault, only the last few characters are ever shown, and prompts and responses are not stored. If that still bothers you, create a separate key with its own spending limit on the provider side and store that one.

It also handles other payments

The original idea behind Saifuban is that agents ask before spending money. Small amounts are approved automatically, and anything above your limit goes to your phone as a notification you can approve or reject. With the API cap on top, most of the ways an agent can spend money are covered.

It's free, there's no email signup, and amounts can be shown in USD or JPY.

If something's missing for your setup, I'd like to hear about it in the comments or on GitHub.

https://github.com/ut181749ut/saifuban

title: How I used parallel Claude Code agents to write hundreds of Chinese working lives
description:
My side project is a game I'm building. This is the side project of that side project.

One Job, One Life is a free browser game. You draw a random job card (a specific job, city, employer and seniority in China) and live it year by year until retirement. You might get a county-hospital surgeon, a deep-sea sailor, or a jianbing street vendor outside a Tianjin metro station.

I built it over a weekend with Claude Code. The interesting part wasn't the app. It was getting a group of agents to write hundreds of careers without the whole thing quietly falling apart. Here is what worked and what broke.

The one decision that shaped everything: no LLM at runtime

Every story is written ahead of time and stored as JSON. While you play, a small seeded rules engine decides what happens: promotions, events, job offers, and when AI starts moving into your tasks.

That means there's no per-play AI cost and no latency, and the same card still plays out differently each run. All the model work moves to authoring time, where I can check it before anyone sees it.

The design idea: the same job title is a different life

A job title tells you surprisingly little. I wanted the game to show that by making you live the difference, so two things are built into the rules.

Place and employer change the whole curve. Each card has a multiplier for its city and employer. Smaller employers also get a lower ceiling: promotions are harder and pay is squeezed further up the ladder. In the simulation, a mid-career neurosurgeon at a top Beijing hospital peaks at about nine times the pay of a new surgeon at a county hospital. Those are modeled estimates, not claims about real people. Place also shows up in the small decisions, like a Beijing renovation manager whose child goes to primary school across the border in Yanjiao.

AI arrives as tasks, not as a robot that takes your job. Each occupation's typical tasks are marked as something AI can do, something shared, or something that stays human. From your third year, AI starts moving in on them one at a time. Most of the time it just changes the work: a film editor's AI rough cut removes a pause, and the editor puts it back. A reporter checks an AI transcript that heard an old woman's Cantonese "don't have" as "have". A tunnel engineer taps the rock with a hammer after a model rated it too highly. When you leave, the review lists what AI still couldn't take.

The game doesn't tell you what to think about any of this. You just live it.

The pipeline

Each career starts from an occupation dataset I've been building: career ladders, pay by years of experience, and a task-by-task assessment of what AI can take.

An agent gets a small batch of jobs and a written brief, then for each one it:

  1. Queries the dataset for that occupation
  2. Writes a draft: a typical day, what each career level is actually like (the daily work, the people, the tools), events, decisions, the backstory and later life
  3. Runs a build script that merges the draft with the real numbers. Agents never type salaries onto the card
  4. Runs a Monte Carlo simulation of hundreds of lives
  5. Writes an English overlay that matches the Chinese card item by item, with numbers inherited rather than retyped

Then validators check it: every level has its story, nothing is missing from the English, no Chinese characters are left over, and the simulated career distribution looks plausible. If nearly everyone reaches the top, the card fails.

Several agents ran at once, each told to touch only its own files.

What went wrong

One agent's mistake became everyone's bug. I added a small feature to the shared build script and put a // comment in the middle of a very long one-line object literal. Everything after it on that line (role, headline, unit, city...) became part of the comment. Every card built in that window silently lost those fields.

An agent noticed, moved the comment and kept going. Afterwards I told agents to report problems with shared scripts instead of editing them, but I was glad this one hadn't waited.

Background agents raced my release. Agents were still building cards while I shipped the finished ones. My release script copied a curated card index into the working tree, then ran git add. Between those two steps an agent's build rewrote the file, so unfinished cards got committed and two deploys failed. The failed builds never went live.

The fix was to stop using the working tree at all and write the file straight into the git index:

git update-index --cacheinfo 100644,$(git hash-object -w "$T/index.ts"),src/lib/game/cards/index.ts

Salary text is hostile. Parsing free-text pay data gave me some great bugs. "3-5 years" became ¥3,000. The 3 in "Unity3D" became a salary. An annual figure read as monthly pay produced someone earning ¥600,000 a month. Each one was found by looking at a simulated result that felt wrong.

The source data was wrong in ways only a careful reader catches. One occupation's AI-exposure tasks described casting turbine blades, but it was a chemical engineer. A sports coach had a physical therapist's career ladder. Agents caught these because they had to write a coherent life on top of the data. They'd write a correction on the card and flag the problem for me.

That became the rule: if you're unsure, skip it, ship what you can confirm, and add it to a doubts list. It kept the work moving, and I reviewed everything in one pass at the end.

My gender checker was confidently wrong. Some stories imply the player's gender, so a script looks for gendered words. It kept flagging 老公房 (an older style of public housing) because it contains 老公, "husband". It also read 陪产假, paternity leave, as a woman's maternity leave. Cheap checks are worth having, but a person or agent still has to read what they flag.

Simulation showed problems no card could fix. On 92% of cards, at least 40% of simulated lives stopped exactly one level below the top, and agents reported that tuning a card barely moved it. On 96% of cards, not one simulated life burned out. Those are engine problems, not writing problems, and they only showed up because every card was simulated.

What I actually did

I set the direction and played the lives. Most of my input was taste: "this is too dark," "this button text is too long," "a foreign player can't read that icon."

To be clear about the AI involved: the code and the stories were written by Claude, and the illustrations came from an image model. The career data is what keeps it grounded, and each event shows where it comes from. This post was drafted with Claude too, from what actually happened during the build, and reviewed by me.

At the end of a life you get a review and a poster:

If you've run content-writing agents at scale, I'd love to hear how you handled shared tooling. And if you try the game, tell me which job you drew and how far you got.

title: Fixing PHP Website Vulnerabilities
description:
Fixing PHP website vulnerabilities requires validating user input, securing sessions, and using secure includes to prevent attacks and protect user data from PHP website vulnerabilities effectively.

Key Takeaways

  • Validate and sanitize user-inputted file uploads to prevent malware uploads and PHP website vulnerabilities.
  • Implement secure session management to prevent session hijacking and fixation, reducing PHP website vulnerabilities.
  • Use secure include practices to prevent remote and local file inclusion attacks and minimize PHP website vulnerabilities.
  • Regularly update and patch PHP and its extensions to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities and PHP website vulnerabilities.

How Does PHP Website Vulnerabilities Work in File Uploads?

PHP website vulnerabilities in file uploads occur when a PHP application allows users to upload files without proper validation and sanitization, enabling attackers to upload malicious files, such as backdoors or shells, which can lead to code execution and server compromise, resulting in PHP website vulnerabilities. To fix this, use the mime_content_type function to check the file type and validate the file extension, as described in the PHP documentation. Additionally, consider using a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to detect and prevent common web attacks, as recommended by the OWASP.

$uploadedFile = $_FILES['file'];
$fileName = $uploadedFile['name'];
$fileType = $uploadedFile['type'];
$fileTemp = $uploadedFile['tmp_name'];

// Validate file type
if ($fileType != 'image/jpeg' && $fileType != 'image/png') {
    echo 'Invalid file type';
    exit;
}

// Validate file extension
$allowedExtensions = array('jpg', 'jpeg', 'png');
$fileExtension = pathinfo($fileName, PATHINFO_EXTENSION);
if (!in_array($fileExtension, $allowedExtensions)) {
    echo 'Invalid file extension';
    exit;
}

Why Are PHP Website Vulnerabilities Critical in Session Management?

PHP website vulnerabilities in session management are essential to prevent session hijacking and fixation attacks, which can allow attackers to access sensitive user data and take control of user accounts, resulting in PHP website vulnerabilities. To implement secure session management and reduce PHP website vulnerabilities, use the session_regenerate_id function to regenerate the session ID after a successful login, and use the session_set_cookie_params function to set the session cookie parameters, such as the lifetime and path, as described in the PHP documentation.

// Regenerate session ID after login
session_regenerate_id(true);

// Set session cookie parameters
session_set_cookie_params(3600, '/; SameSite=Lax', 'example.com', true, true);

How Do PHP Website Vulnerabilities Occur in Insecure Includes?

PHP website vulnerabilities in insecure includes occur when a PHP application includes files without proper validation and sanitization, enabling attackers to include remote or local files, which can lead to code execution and server compromise, resulting in PHP website vulnerabilities. To fix this and minimize PHP website vulnerabilities, use the include statement with a validated and sanitized file path, and avoid using user-inputted data in the include statement, as recommended by the PHP documentation.

// Validated and sanitized file path
$filePath = 'includes/header.php';

// Include the file
include $filePath;

What Are the Best Practices for Preventing PHP Website Vulnerabilities?

To prevent PHP website vulnerabilities, it is essential to follow best practices, such as validating and sanitizing user input, implementing secure session management, and using secure include practices. Additionally, regularly update and patch PHP and its extensions to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities and PHP website vulnerabilities. Consider using a security framework, such as OWASP ESAPI, to provide an additional layer of security and protect against PHP website vulnerabilities.

How Can I Stay Up-to-Date with the Latest PHP Website Vulnerabilities?

To stay up-to-date with the latest PHP website vulnerabilities, it is essential to regularly check the PHP documentation and the OWASP website for the latest security advisories and best practices. Additionally, consider subscribing to security newsletters and attending security conferences to stay informed about the latest PHP website vulnerabilities and security threats.

Related Guides

  • PHP 8 Upgrade
  • Securing Legacy PHP Applications
  • Achieving GDPR Compliance

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the most common PHP website vulnerability?

The most common PHP website vulnerability is the file upload vulnerability, which can be exploited by uploading malicious files, resulting in PHP website vulnerabilities, and can be prevented by validating and sanitizing user-inputted file uploads.

How can I prevent session hijacking attacks and reduce PHP website vulnerabilities?

You can prevent session hijacking attacks and reduce PHP website vulnerabilities by implementing secure session management, such as regenerating the session ID after a successful login and setting the session cookie parameters, as described in the PHP documentation.

What is the best way to secure include statements and minimize PHP website vulnerabilities?

The best way to secure include statements and minimize PHP website vulnerabilities is to use a validated and sanitized file path, and avoid using user-inputted data in the include statement, as recommended by the PHP documentation, and to regularly update and patch PHP and its extensions to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities and PHP website vulnerabilities.
